# Book Two · Chapter 1: Nothing to sign with
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.8 · EN

## Day One Hundred and Fifty · Monday 2 March

Two things ran out, a day apart, and they pulled in opposite directions.

The sentence from the second of January ran out when March did, and March came in on the Sunday. He spent the end of that Sunday on the floor at a window, against her legs, and it did not once occur to him that he was free to go and look at somebody.

The instrument died at midnight at the end of that same Sunday, on the date he had asked for himself.

So on the Monday he was permitted to work and had nothing to work with.

Mrs Seo's tray went up at seven, the way it has gone up at seven since October.

The staff table was laid for four and sat six. The boy from the kitchens ate standing at the end of it, because Mr Baek had never told him to sit down and had never once told him not to.

Yun had been in the house eight weeks. In January he carried plates on his forearms. In March he carried them in his hands, and nobody in that kitchen had said a word to him about it.

The boy said good morning to him, and had said it every day since the second week, which nobody had told him to do either. Two of the four maids still do not.

Georgij had graded him in the first week and had had nothing to add since the middle of February.

This was the third Monday running on which he had come down early enough to watch another man work.

She was in the small room at eight with her coat over the back of the chair.

The same chair and the same hour as the second of January. On the second of January she had been sitting in it an hour before the car with nothing in front of her, waiting for him to come past. This morning she was working, and he was the one who came.

"Mistress."

"It is March," said Annie.

"Yes."

"On the twenty-seventh of November I asked you for the smallest instrument that works, with a date on it, and I said that after the date it would be dead and I would ask you again." He stopped inside the door and stayed there. "It died at midnight."

Annie put down the page she was holding and did not turn it face down.

"Ask, then."

"I am asking."

"What for?"

Georgij had his hands at his sides.

"On the twenty-third of January a renewal in Jung-gu came up against a date and you were in Yeouido until nine. Two pages came up the drive on a scooter. I put a name on them and it took four minutes."

"That is what it turned out to be for."

"Yes."

"Then I will give one to Mrs Seo." Annie sat back. "Nine years in this house. She runs the staff and the accounts and the outside firms, and when a man on a scooter comes up that drive at six in the evening she is already in the building. It costs me one afternoon in Jung-gu and it does not expire."

There was nothing wrong with any part of that.

"Yes, Mistress."

"Say the rest of it."

"There is no rest of it that I can put a figure against."

Annie turned her chair a few degrees, so that she was facing him and not the desk.

"Mr Chae told you in December that the instrument was smaller than you thought it was. Yesterday he told you he had never been that exactly right about one before."

"He did."

"He was right about the size of it, and he does not know what you wanted it for." Her hands were still on the arms of the chair. "I do. So do you. Neither of us has said it out loud, and one of us is about to."

Georgij did not have anywhere to put his hands and put them behind his back.

"In November, in the office at the end of a shed at Yeongjong, you told an old man that you had nothing to sign with. You said it was not modesty. You said it was the arrangement."

"I did."

"There is no arrangement."

Her coat was still over the back of the chair.

"There is a set of papers your compliance people tidied up in the second week of October," said Georgij. "My name is on them. Yours is not."

Annie waited.

"There was a line in a book with an owner on it and a date, and my name was not on that either, because there is no column for it." His hands stayed where they were. "The instrument that died at midnight had both. It is the only thing that ever has."

Annie got up and took the coat off the back of the chair.

"Mr Chae draws instruments with counterparties in them. He asks what it is for, he writes the answer down, and it goes into a leather case and into a room in Jung-gu, and in twenty years a stranger reads it." She had the coat over her arm and did not put it on. "What you have just said to me is not a thing that goes in a case."

"No, Mistress."

"Then ask me again when there is a room in it."

She went out past him with the coat over her arm, the way she had gone out past him on the second of January.

At the door she stopped, which she had not done then.

"You are working again," said Annie. "Nobody has told you what to want."

Georgij stayed where he was for a moment after she had gone.

On the second of January he had come off the stairs with a reason inside ten minutes, and he had been satisfied with it for about a week, and it had been wrong for eight of them.

This morning he had nothing at all. That is not the same thing as having nothing to do, and he had spent the winter learning the difference.

* * *

The catalogue came at eleven in a flat parcel with a printed label, addressed to the house and not to anybody in it.

Mrs Seo put it on the desk in the small room with three other things. It lay there until two. Annie was in Yeouido, and there was no reason on earth for Georgij to be in that room.

He went in at two.

He picked it up, which he had not done in October.

In October it had lain forty centimetres from his hand at the corner of that desk. He had read it upside down at twenty-two seconds a page and Annie had counted. Neither of them had said out loud what he was looking for.

It was the same size and the same weight. The paper was better.

The house used to renumber every month, so a number meant nothing at all. He had worked that out in October in the time it takes to go down one page, and knowing that a number means nothing is the kind of thing a man keeps.

The numbers had stopped meaning nothing.

At the foot of the first page, in six point, under a rule that had not been there before:

*References are permanent and are not reissued. Withdrawn and completed entries retain their reference.*

He went down the descriptions the way he had gone down them in October, which takes a particular kind of reading, because the whole thing is written in the flat abbreviated language of a livestock list.

Female, twenty-eight. Male, thirty, with a trade. Male, twenty-four, with a mark against him for a second return.

The mark goes in the book now and it stays there, and the man it is against will carry it into every room he is ever stood up in.

Nineteen lots.

He read the whole of it once. He did not read it a second time backwards, the way you check figures, because in October he had been looking for somebody and this morning he was not.

At the back there was a page that had never been at the back of anything in that house.

It was a list and it went back four years. A reference, a season, and one word.

The references were not catalogue numbers. Catalogue numbers are made up fresh every month and thrown away when the month is over. These were the numbers out of the book. They stand in a column with an owner and a date beside them, and he had looked at one of them yesterday morning on a photocopy with a grey smear at either end.

*Completed* against most of them. *Withdrawn* against some.

And against four of them, in the same six point, three words in place of the one.

*Retained, not disclosed.*

He found eleven, and then he found fourteen, four lines further down in the same column, with the same three words against both.

Four in four years. Two of them were hers.

Under the list there was a short paragraph about the keeping of records, and at the bottom of the page a name and a title.

He read the paragraph twice, which he had not needed to do with anything else in that book.

It was four sentences long and every one of them was about method. References are permanent. Entries are retained. The practice is reviewed once a year and the review is minuted. Prior seasons have been brought into the same series.

Nowhere in the four sentences was there a word about what the references were references to.

His chin did what it does in front of work that is better than it has to be. There was nobody in the room to see it, and the work was a paragraph about filing.

Georgij put the book down and squared it to the edge of the desk.

Then he stood in that room and did the arithmetic he had been putting off since the foot of the first page.

A reference that is never reissued cannot be taken back. A gap in that list is a gap for as long as the list exists. Every gap carries a season beside it. The list goes out in a flat parcel to everybody who buys.

The line was struck on the nineteenth of February. The striking of it is now the most durable thing about it.

Yesterday he had told her that what was round his neck went on working for exactly as long as nobody looked in that book.

Somebody had made the book portable. It had come up the drive that morning in a flat parcel with a printed label on it.

* * *

Annie came back from Yeouido at ten past eight.

The catalogue was where he had left it, closed and square to the edge, with the other three things beside it.

"You have read it," said Annie.

"Yes."

She took her coat off, put it over the back of the chair, and sat down in the chair she sits in.

"They kept the numbers," said Georgij. "In October a number meant nothing, because they renumbered every month. Now a number is a number for good, and the ones that are gone are printed with the ones that are not, so that a buyer can see that nothing has been quietly lost."

"I know what is on that page."

"Eleven and fourteen. Four lines apart, the same three words against each."

"I know which two they are."

Georgij stayed on the far side of the desk.

"You paid to have a line struck out of a book, and the book has begun printing a list of the lines that have been struck out of it."

"Yes."

"Then it is worth more tonight than it was in October." His hands were at his sides again. "Whoever owns that book has the name of every person in this country who has ever paid to make a line go away. There are four lines. I am one of them."

Annie looked at the window and not at the desk, and for a while she did not say anything at all.

"There is a name at the bottom of that page," said Georgij.

"There is."

"Did you meet him?"

Annie put her hand flat on the arm of the chair.

"Ask me something else."

He asked her about the haulier in Gimpo. It was four lines on a sheet she had turned face down in January without a word, and it was two months stale now, and worth about half of what it had been.

She answered him for twenty minutes, in detail, and sent him to find out two things he could only find out by going and looking at somebody.

Neither of them said anything more that evening about the page at the back of the book.

In November he had stood in an office at the end of a shed with the sea on three sides of it. He had told an old man that he had nothing to sign with, and that it was not modesty, it was the arrangement.

It was the first evening on which only the first half of that was true.

# Book Two · Chapter 2: The order of loading
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.6 · EN

## Day One Hundred and Fifty-Two · Wednesday 4 March

Mr Ku drove him out to Gimpo on the Wednesday morning and did not ask what for.

The two drivers used to go week and week about. That has stopped, without anybody saying so: Mr Pyo has her, and Mr Ku has him.

The yard was off a road with three yards on it and the other two were bigger. Room for eight and four trucks in it. One of the four had its bonnet up, and there was rain standing in the engine bay, so it had been up since the weekend and nobody had put anything over it.

Shin came out himself. There was nobody to send.

Georgij had four ways of opening with a man he needed something from. He stood in that yard for about three seconds and put all four of them down.

Three were for rooms in which the other man was still deciding what Georgij was. Shin was not deciding anything about anybody. He was standing in his own gate in March with four trucks and five weeks of nothing coming. There is no version of charm that does not read, to a man in that position, as somebody from a large house enjoying himself.

The fourth was the question about who to be careful of, and that one belongs to a newcomer.

You cannot take anything from a man who has nothing. You can only pay him.

So he paid first, before he had asked for anything, which is not an order he had ever used.

"You lost Daehan at the end of January," said Georgij. "I am going to tell you why. Then I am going to ask you two things, and you can decide afterwards whether you answer them."

Shin wiped his hands down the front of his coat and said nothing at all.

"It was not you. It was not your price and it was not the two loads in October." He gave it flat and in order, the way he gives everything. "In August their insurer rewrote one line about carrier concentration. Above a tonnage they may use one named haulier and only one, from the first of January. You are under the tonnage. Nobody at your size in this country kept that contract this year, and the man who took it off you is not better at this than you are."

Shin stood there for a while.

"I went and asked them," he said. "Twice. Second time a fellow came out to the car park to tell me there was nothing to tell me."

"There was nothing he was permitted to tell you." Georgij took a folded sheet out of his coat and put it into Shin's hand. "It is in their own filing and it has been public since August. Page twenty-six. The paragraph is four lines long and your name is not in it."

Shin looked at the sheet in his own hand and then at the yard.

"I put two men off in February," he said.

"I know."

"I told them both it was the two loads in October." He said it evenly enough. "That's what I had."

Georgij did not tell him that he could go and say something else to those two men now. A man who has just been handed a page works that out on his own, and saying it out loud would have been the second thing given and the first thing taken.

Shin put the sheet away in an inside pocket without unfolding it, which was what Georgij had expected.

"Ask your two," he said.

The first was what he still had. Four trucks running and a fifth that would run for the price of a pump. The yard on a lease with two years left on it. Two licences that take a year and a half to get, and he had held both for twelve years. One of the two is the whole reason anybody in Seoul would ever look at a road haulier in Gimpo.

The second was what he owed, and Shin gave him that one at the same speed, which not one man in four does.

It was worse than the four lines Annie had turned face down in January had assumed. It was also all in one place, to one lender, and secured on the trucks and not on the licences, which is the difference between a man who is finished and a man who is having a bad year.

Georgij wrote none of it down while he was standing there.

Georgij thanked him for them and did not ask anything else.

Shin went on anyway, walking him back over the yard, and this was the part that was not in anybody's note.

"You want to know what it's actually like now, go and stand at the Incheon gate at four in the morning." Shin had his hands in his coat pockets. "I'm there twice a week. Twelve years. It's not the same yard it was in November."

"What is different?"

"The order of loading." Shin stopped walking. "Nine months of the year that place is full. It has always been full and everybody has always waited, and waiting is the job. What's different since January is that the waiting has a shape to it. Same name goes on first. Every sailing. And there's three or four of us who've worked that out from being one of the ones that doesn't."

"There's a fellow out of Ulsan I've known eight years. Chemicals. One lane, nothing else, never had anything else." Shin was looking at his own trucks and not at Georgij. "His boxes have rolled twice since the middle of January. Two sailings. He doesn't sleep at home any more. He sleeps in the cab at the gate on a Tuesday night so he's first through in the morning. He's one of six on that lane and not one of the six is big enough to be told anything. There's an association of some sort that writes letters and I couldn't tell you who signs them."

He turned his head.

"Being first through that gate has got nothing whatever to do with what goes on the ship. He knows that. He does it anyway."

"Somebody bought something over the winter," said Shin. "Nobody knows what and nobody in Gimpo is ever going to be told. But you can read it off the quay, and it reads the same every week."

Georgij stood in a yard in Gimpo with the rain going into an engine bay eight metres away and read his own handwriting off a stranger's account of a Tuesday night.

He had written it out in November at a dining table with three people sitting at it. *A veto over routes decides which container goes on which sailing when a sailing is full.* He had said it out loud, in that order, and he had been pleased with how clean it was.

He had put it forward as a reason to do it.

A man sleeps in a cab now, on the strength of it.

At the gate Shin asked what house he was from, which is what a man asks when he does not want to ask for a name.

"Hers is not on anything you have read," said Georgij. "I advise one person, and I have done it for less than a year."

"And she wants my trucks."

"She wants to know what is in this yard. What is done about it is not decided, and I would not tell you if it were."

Shin took that the way a man takes the first straight answer he has had since January, which it may well have been.

Mr Ku had the engine on before Georgij reached the car, because it was cold and because that is the standard of the man.

Georgij sat in the back with nothing in his hands for most of the way and did the arithmetic on it instead.

He had given a stranger in Gimpo a piece of reasoning that perhaps four people in this country would have gone and done, and he had given it away unasked, on a Wednesday, for two facts about trucks.

It was the correct trade. He had been in that yard under a minute when he understood it was the only trade on offer there, and he had made it, and it had come back at about six times what he went for.

It also has a shape. A man who pays in one particular currency, three times, has signed something.

* * *

Annie came out of the small room at half past eight.

He gave her the two things first, because those were the things that had been asked for, and she had them in under a minute and did not look surprised by either.

"And I paid him for them," said Georgij. "Before I asked, not after."

Annie did not put anything down.

"He lost Daehan at the end of January because of one line in an insurer's requirement, and he has spent five weeks believing it was his own fault. I told him it was not. I left him the page."

"It cost you nothing." He had not sat down. "It is public, it has been public since August, and there are perhaps four people in this country who would have gone and read it in order to answer that particular question. That is the part that cost something. He will repeat it, and he will repeat where he had it."

Annie looked at him for a moment.

"What else?"

So he gave her the gate at four in the morning, and the shape of the waiting, and the man out of Ulsan who sleeps in a cab on a Tuesday night.

She took that one differently. She sat down for it, in her own chair, and she asked him six questions.

Two of them he could not answer. One was how long the Ulsan one had been rolling before Shin noticed, which nobody at that gate would know and which decides whether it is eight weeks of trouble or five months of it. The other was whether anybody had gone to him yet.

"How many are there like him?"

"Shin says three or four out of Gimpo alone, and Gimpo is one road with three yards on it." Georgij was still standing. "I do not know the number. I know the mechanism, because I wrote it out for you at a table in November and I was pleased with it at the time."

"You wrote it out correctly," said Annie.

"I did."

"And you are telling me that it works."

"I am telling you that it works exactly as far as we said it would." He turned his hand over. "And about four hundred metres further than anybody at that table went to look."

Annie did not argue with any part of that, which he had not expected either.

"Bring me the name on that lane," she said. "Not from Shin. From the filings, and then from somebody who has stood at that gate."

"Yes, Mistress."

She was already going back into the small room when she stopped.

"You will find that they are all four of them worth having, and that two of them will be gone by June." Her hand was on the frame. "That is not a reason to hurry. It is the shape of the thing."

Later, on the stairs, he worked out that she had said nothing at all about the page he had left in a yard in Gimpo.

Not yes. Not no. Not that it was hers to leave.

That was the second time in two days that a question he had put down in front of her had been stepped over rather than answered, and the first time had been about a name.

Yesterday he had asked her for a piece of paper saying what he was permitted to do, and she had not given him one.

Today he had given something of hers to a stranger without one, and had been right, and she had let it stand.

He went up the east stairs and did not count them.

# Book Two · Chapter 3: We haven't met
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.5 · EN

## Day One Hundred and Fifty-Five · Saturday 7 March

Nobody had asked him for any of it.

On the Wednesday night Annie had asked for the name on that lane, from the filings and then from somebody who had stood at that gate. That is three days of work for a man who is quick, and he had it by Thursday afternoon.

He spent Thursday evening, Friday and Saturday on something else.

He closed the Ulsan file at about four on the Thursday and had three days in front of him with nothing in them.

On the Monday she had stopped at the door on her way out and told him he was working again, and that nobody had told him what to want. She had meant it as a release. He had taken it as one, and he is fairly certain she did not mean this.

Then he went down and took the catalogue off the desk in the small room and carried it upstairs, which is the first thing he has ever taken out of that room without being handed it.

What he had was four references and three seasons, and no column for who paid.

Two of the references were the fourth of October. Eleven and fourteen, four lines apart, and he had been in the room for both of them and had been one of them.

The other two were older. One was three years back. One was the year before that.

The house was never going to tell him anything and he did not go near it.

What he went at instead was the outside of an evening.

An auction of that kind is four hours in a building with a public stair and a private entrance. The people who come to it arrive in cars that somebody has to park and to wait in. The men who wait get fed at somebody's expense and then invoiced for. There is a settlement desk and there are runners who go down to the seats. There is a florist. There is a firm that puts out the chairs and takes them away again.

None of those people are in the book. All of them have their own paper, and their paper has dates on it.

He had done this once before, in his first fortnight, for a charity gala with eight hundred people at it, and it had given him four hundred and thirty names and had not given him Choi Dae-ho.

He did it again for an evening three years old.

He did it at the desk in his own room, which has a window on the east side and a lamp that Mrs Seo replaced in November without being asked and without mentioning it.

The boy brought a tray up on the Friday at one because nobody had come down. He put it at the corner of the desk on the side where there was room, which is a thing that has to be worked out and not taught.

Georgij thanked him and did not look up, and that was the whole of the human part of Friday.

It took Friday and most of Saturday and it worked.

Cars, in the end. A firm in Jung-gu that supplies drivers by the hour keeps its dockets for seven years, on account of a tax dispute it lost and has not got over. A docket carries a pick-up address and a drop. A drop that is the same street four times in three years is a customer.

Then the drop is a building, and the building has one tenant that receives people in the evening.

Then it is a matter of which of the four dockets falls on the right night, and after that of whose account the hours went to.

The account was a company. The company was a nothing, two rooms and a secretary, and it took Georgij about an hour to get behind it because whoever set it up had not been trying very hard, which by itself said something.

Behind it was a woman of eighty-one who has been charming for forty years and has never in that time told anybody anything all the way through.

Georgij put the sheet down on the desk and did not do any more work for a while.

He had shaken her hand in a ballroom on the twenty-fifth of October. She had come at him from the left at the ten-minute mark. Three weeks before that she had sat two rows in front of the woman who bought him, and had turned round with everybody else when a man in the second row stood up.

*We haven't met.*

He had thought at the time that it was a courtesy, and that she was giving him the evening clean because she was the sort of woman who understood what an entrance costs.

It was not a courtesy. It was a woman with something on that page, being extremely careful in front of a man who had just come off it.

He worked out on Saturday afternoon what she had actually been doing, and it took him under a minute once he stopped being flattered.

She had not been protecting him. She had been finding out, in four words and without asking, whether the new one at that table knew what she was.

He had told her, with his face, that he did not. She had given him six or seven minutes of nothing at all after that and had gone away pleased.

What he does not have, and will not get out of a docket, is what was on the line.

A reference, a season and a stroke of a pen. Somebody stood in that building three years ago with a number over their head, and a woman of eighty-one bought them, and then paid a second time to have the fact taken out of the book.

There are two reasons a person pays for that, and one of them is the reason Annie had. From the outside of an evening they look exactly alike.

The other one, the fourth, is not there.

Nobody ordered a car. Nobody was fed. The chair firm invoiced for the room and the florist invoiced for the room and there is no third piece of paper anywhere with that evening on it.

Georgij went at it twice and then put it down and wrote a line to himself about the age of the records, which was reasonable.

He had three of the four and one name out of two, and the name is the wrong half.

Deterrence needs the other side of it. A page with Annie on it and a woman of eighty-one on it is a page with two people on it who can both be hurt, and that is not a deadlock, that is a queue.

What he needs is somebody so large that the page cannot be used at all, and that one is the one with no car, no dinner and no paper.

He considered going to her, for about as long as it takes to put a cup down.

Against it: she is eighty-one and has been careful since before he was born, and a woman like that gets warned once. Walk up her drive with that page in your head and she knows within a sentence that somebody has read it, and after that she is careful about a specific thing instead of about everything, which is worse.

For it: nothing at all. He has no currency she wants. He is a man with no money who has already given her, in a ballroom, the one piece of information she went there to get.

So it is one approach and he has not got it ready, and the rule for that is the one Hana said out loud on a Thursday in November about a different woman who receives nobody. Not quickly and not twice.

* * *

Annie came in at nine with the Yeouido people gone and her coat already off.

He gave her Ulsan.

The name is Nam Byung-hee. She has the firm, which is one lane and nothing else, and she has run it since her brother died. She also has the chair of the association of independent shippers on that lane, which has existed for twenty years and which nobody has ever wanted before, because until January there was nothing on that lane to negotiate about.

Six firms. She writes to them on the first of every month whether there is anything to write about or not.

Georgij had that last part from a man who has stood at the gate, which is what had been asked for.

Annie went through it and asked four things.

Two were about the six firms. One was about the association's own constitution, which he had read on the Thursday. It is mostly nothing, apart from a single clause about who may speak for the members in a dealing with a carrier.

The fourth was whether Nam Byung-hee had ever held anything outside this trade, and the answer is no, and Annie put her hand flat on the arm of the chair when she heard it.

"She writes on the first," she said.

"Every month. Twenty years of it. The last three say nothing, and she sent them anyway."

Annie looked at that for a moment.

"Then she is not somebody who is going to be told to be patient."

"No, Mistress."

"What have you been doing since Thursday afternoon?"

Georgij had known the question was coming since about four o'clock and had decided what he was going to do about it, and doing it turned out to be worse than deciding it.

"Something of my own. I will tell you, and I am not going to tell you tonight."

Annie did not move at all.

"Is it going to cost me anything?"

"Not yet. On the day it starts to, you will have all of it that day, and you will not have to ask me for it."

"And if I ask you now."

"Then I will tell you now." He said that at the same speed as the rest of it. "I would rather you did not ask, and I am saying so instead of letting you find it out."

The clock in the hall did the thing it does at the quarter.

"Keep it, then," said Annie.

She went past him and put her hand on the back of his neck on the way, the way she had twice in February, and went straight on to whatever she had been going to.

He stood in the hall afterwards and did the arithmetic, because he does.

He had given her a term. Not tonight, and on the day it costs you, and if you ask I will tell you. Three limits on a thing he was keeping back, all of them said out loud, all of them binding on him and on nobody else.

That is how he does it. He has done it since October: a ceiling, named counterparties, a date after which it is dead and I ask you again.

In six days she had stepped over two of his questions and had not put a date on either.

He went up and did not make anything of it. There is nothing to make of it that would survive being said out loud. And a man who counts what he is owed by the person he belongs to has started keeping a different sort of book.

He got as far as the landing before he heard which word he had used.

*Belongs.* On the seventh of March, by a man with no line, no owner and no date anywhere in the world.

He did not correct it.

---

# Book Two · Chapter 4: I have nothing to put in it
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.10 · EN

## Day One Hundred and Fifty-Nine · Wednesday 11 March

He did not go looking for the man. He went looking for the calendar.

A man with thirty-one years in a trade that size is on a schedule whether he likes it or not, and most of it is private and about four days of it a year are not. Launches. Handovers. The opening of somebody else's terminal.

And funerals.

They are announced, and that is all it takes. A death in that trade goes into two papers and onto a hall's own board, with the room number and the three days, and anybody at all may come.

Georgij found one on the Sunday night in about twenty minutes.

The man had been seventy-six. He had run a coastal feeder line out of Mokpo for most of his life, sold it to somebody larger six years ago, and gone on going to things afterwards, which is what men do.

Georgij had never met him. He read what there was and it took under an hour, and at the end of it he knew four true things about a man he was going to use.

Mr Ku drove him and did not ask, again.

The hall was on the third floor and there was a queue at the desk outside the room, and the queue was moving because these things move.

At the desk there is a book.

Everybody who comes writes his name in it. Then he puts an envelope in the box beside it, and the amount goes in the book too, in the second column, in a different hand, later.

Georgij stood in the queue and understood at about the fourth person what he had walked into.

He had known there would be a book. He had not thought about the box, because he does not think about money, because thinking about money has never once been useful to him.

He wrote his name.

It is not a thing he has done often. There were papers in the second week of October so that he could sign, and there was an instrument in December, and both of those were his name on a line about what he was permitted to do.

This was a book with a name in it and nothing else next to it.

The man at the desk had one hand out for the envelope and was already looking past him at the next in the queue.

"I have nothing to put in it," said Georgij.

The hand stopped.

There is a particular quality to that half-second. Contempt would be easier. It is a man recalculating what he is looking at, in a good coat, at a funeral, in a queue.

"That is all right," he said, in the end.

"It is not. I am telling you because you will write it in the second column and somebody will think it was a mistake." Georgij did not move out of the way yet. "It was not a mistake. Put a line through it."

The man put a line through it.

Then Georgij went in and bowed twice and came out again, which took about ninety seconds and which he did properly, because a room like that is the last one in which a man ought to be economical.

* * *

Park Sang-hoon was in the corridor at the end, near the window where the smokers stand, with two men who wanted things from him and were not going to get them today.

He had seen Georgij come out of the room. He had probably seen him in the queue.

He came over himself, which was the whole reason it had to be a room and not a telephone.

"Two billion two hundred million," said Sang-hoon.

"Chairman."

"Mr Georgij. I have thought about it since December and I have not moved off it, and I am not going to." He had a paper cup of something he was not drinking. "I have moved up. Say a number."

Georgij put his hands behind his back.

"He was never for sale," he said. "Five words. They were hers and not mine, and I was in the room when she said them."

"I remember who was in the room."

"And thank you." He said it without any decoration on it at all. "You have not moved off that figure from December to March. On the day you set it you gave her a reason for it, and the reason was a thing you had watched me do."

"I remember what I said."

"So do I. It is the only compliment anybody has ever paid me that arrived with a number on it. I have thought about that more than is useful. And I would sooner have had it from you than from anybody in this country."

Sang-hoon laughed at that, once, and two men down the corridor looked over and then looked away again.

"It was higher than the one that is on anybody," he said. "That is the part your side has never understood. I do not pay what a thing is worth. I pay what it costs to stop having to think about it."

Then he stopped, and he looked at Georgij for slightly too long, and he did not say the next thing.

Georgij watched him not say it, and had a fair idea what it was, because there is only one fact about him that a man in that position would hold back and enjoy holding back.

It went across Sang-hoon's face for about a quarter of a second. Then it was gone, and it was still his.

"You did not come here for a man from Mokpo," said Sang-hoon.

"No."

"You did not know him."

"I did not know him. I read four things about him on Sunday night and came here on the strength of them." Georgij went on before he was asked. "You come to these. There is no other room in this country I can walk into and find you in."

"You could have written to me."

"Then you would have had a day to decide what I wanted."

Sang-hoon put the cup down on the sill.

"Ask."

"You will have had somebody look in a book for you, in a building near the river." Georgij said it flat. "A man who puts a figure on a thing and does not move off it from December to March has been at the paper on it. I do not want what was on the page. I want to know how you got the look."

That was the whole of the ask, and Sang-hoon took about four seconds over it, which for him is a long time.

"You want to know whether the door is still there."

"Yes."

"It is there. It is not going to be there in a month." He was not enjoying himself, which was new. "They have a new man. He has been through the room where they keep it and he has been through the people, and the ones who were useful were useful because nobody had ever looked at them."

"Who?"

"Settlement." Sang-hoon watched two men go past with their coats over their arms. "There is always somebody in settlement. It is the only desk in the building that touches every line and gets paid the least for it, and it has been that way in every one of these places since before either of us was born."

"And the price?"

"For me it was not money." He turned round. "And that is what you have come for, so we can stop walking round it. What do you have?"

Georgij had known since Sunday what he had.

"You want to know how it was done."

"I know how it was done. I have had two and a half months and I am not stupid." Sang-hoon's voice did not go up. "I know the report was true. I know the board could not sell, and I asked you about it myself, in the middle of a conversation about a ceiling, and it was not on any page you gave me, and I bought it anyway. I have been over that evening more times than I have been over anything since I was thirty."

He put one finger down on the sill.

"What I do not have is why I bought it. I saw the wall. I asked you about it out loud, at your table, and then I signed."

The window was open two inches at the top and the corridor was cold at that end and somebody in the room behind them was crying properly, without any performance in it.

"Why it was you is the half you have had since December," said Georgij. "You were going to take the Kim logistics and she could not let you. There is nothing else in that part of it. If you had been after a chemical works I would have gone and found you a chemical works."

"I know why it was me. I am not asking you that."

"No."

"Then take the rest in order." The two men down the corridor gave up and went away. "You would have bought Hanseong Shipping from anybody. Routes, cheap, bleeding, and half a board that wants out will sign inside a fortnight. That is your trade, and it is the only reason the thing could be used at all."

"And I would have looked at the other half of that board."

"You would have looked at it for ten minutes and walked away, and I would have had nothing." He did not hurry any of it. "You did not look, because it was never in front of you as a thing to buy."

"On the eighteenth of November you talked to me for three and a half hours about how you work," said Georgij. "You were pleased to do it. I did not ask you one question I had not decided on in a car on the way there."

"Go on."

"You told me that when you take hold of a thing you do not put it down. You said it as a virtue, because it is one, and it is the reason you have what you have." He did not stop. "It is also the only part of you that can be aimed. Everything else is judgement, and judgement will not go where a stranger points it."

"So I did not put it in front of you as an opportunity. I put nineteen true pages in front of you and asked you whether the whole of it was nonsense, because you had more idea than I did."

Sang-hoon did not say anything for a while.

"It was you being wrong," he said.

"Page nine." Georgij held his eye. "Two rumours about money missing at a subsidiary, one from a shipping agent and one from a woman who audits and has never met him. I had them as two sources and I put my weight on them. You wrote one word beside it."

"Same."

"One mouth, walked round the long way and back. I received it at both ends and counted it twice, and I was pleased with myself for four days."

"That is the part I want you to have straight," said Georgij. "It was a real mistake and I did not know it was there. I did not need to know. I needed the nineteen pages to be true and the asking to be genuine, and both of those were."

"I found four," said Sang-hoon. "In pencil. I read the nineteen pages twice to do it, and I said so to her at her own door, because it was worth saying."

"Then somewhere in the second reading you stopped correcting a report."

"Say what I was doing."

"Winning." Georgij turned his hand over. "You had it won by page eleven, and there was nothing to show for it except three words and a figure in a margin. A man like you does not leave a thing won and unpaid."

"You were not valuing an asset when you signed. You had finished the argument two weeks earlier and you were putting the last word on it, and the last word cost several hundred billion won."

"And you knew that on the eighteenth."

"I knew it about forty minutes in. I stayed for the other two hours and fifty because it was the best thing anybody has ever told me about this trade, and I was enjoying it. I want that said, because it is the part I am least comfortable with."

Sang-hoon looked out of the window at a car park.

"Then I gave it to you," he said.

"You gave it to me. I went and got it, and you handed it over, and both of those are true and neither of them cancels the other."

"You know what the worst of it is." It was not a question and it did not get a mark. "I would do the three and a half hours again. With you, next week, if you asked. That is not a man who has learned something. That is a man who found out what he is."

He had said the worst thing a man in his position can say about himself, and he had said it to somebody with nothing to trade it to.

"The name in settlement," said Sang-hoon, after a while, "is not one I am going to say in a corridor with a funeral in it."

"No."

"Come out to the car."

They went down, and it took four minutes. What Georgij came out with fitted into one line of a notebook, and he did not take the notebook out until he was in the back of his own car with the door shut.

Sang-hoon had one more thing at the car door, and he said it as though it had only just occurred to him, which with him it never has.

"When she is finished with you," he said, "you will not come to me. I know that, and I am not asking you to."

"Chairman."

"Mr Georgij." He had the door open and did not get in yet. "I am telling you where I am. Four or five of these a year, until I am the one in the room. You will not have to write to anybody. You will not have to ask a man for a favour or stand in an office and be looked at. You come and stand in a corridor, and I will come over, and it will cost you nothing to find out whether I am still saying this."

"Why?"

"Because I have wanted to buy you twice and been told no twice, and both times I went home and thought about the work and not about the price." He got in. "That is the whole of it. A man should say a thing like that once and then not go on about it."

* * *

Jang met the car on the gravel, which he does not do.

He did not say anything and he did not need to. He had known since half past nine where a car of that house had gone. A hall of that kind publishes the room number and the three days. And knowing where the cars go is his job, and he has never once been bad at it.

Annie was in the small room with the door open.

Georgij stood in it with his coat still on and did the only arithmetic that mattered. It took no time at all.

He had come home to tell her. She had it first. There is no version of the next ten minutes in which he can prove the order.

He had said it out loud on Saturday. *On the day it starts to cost you, you will have all of it that day.*

The trouble with a man who has never said anything untrue is that he has also never had to be believed.

"Take the coat off," said Annie.

---

# Book Two · Chapter 5: The east side
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.11 · EN

## Day One Hundred and Fifty-Nine · Wednesday 11 March

He took the coat off and put it over the arm of the chair by the door, and then he did the difficult part first, because leaving it any later would have turned it into something.

"Jang was on the gravel," he said. "He does not stand out there, and knowing where the cars of this house go is his job. There is no way for me to show you which of us was going to say it first."

"No."

"I am not going to try. I would only be asking you to take my word for the one thing my word is no good for."

Annie was at the window with the curtain not drawn and the drive dark behind the glass.

"The order is not what is wrong with today," she said. "Give me all of it."

He gave it in order and it took twelve minutes.

The catalogue off the desk in the small room. Four references and three seasons and no column for who paid. Two of them the fourth of October, four lines apart. Two of them older, one three years back, one the year before that.

Then the outside of an evening. A firm in Jung-gu that keeps its dockets for seven years on account of a tax dispute it lost. A drop that is the same street four times in three years. A company with two rooms and a secretary and nobody behind it who had been trying very hard.

Then the name.

"Sunwoo," said Annie.

"On the older of the two. I have not got the other one."

"You will not." She did not say it as a challenge. "Go on."

"The fourth is not there at all. No car, no dinner, no third piece of paper. The chair firm invoiced for the room and the florist invoiced for the room and that is the whole of the evening."

"And you put that down to the records."

"I put it down to the age of the records on Saturday, and I wrote myself a line saying so." He did not decorate it. "It was reasonable and it is probably wrong. Nobody eats and nobody parks. That is not an old evening, that is an arranged one."

Annie let that stand for a moment, and then she asked her first real question, which was not about any of it.

"What did you pay Park Sang-hoon with?"

"Hanseong Shipping. All of it. Why he signed after he had seen the wall, and how the report was put in front of him, and what it was in him that could be aimed."

"Every part of it."

"Every part. He had two and a half months on it and he had the half that anybody could get. I gave him the other half in a corridor in about six minutes."

She did not say anything about that at all, which she had not in February either, and he had learned by now not to take the silence as either of the two things it looks like.

"And in return."

"There is a desk in settlement. There is always somebody in settlement, because it is the only desk in a building of that kind that touches every line and gets paid the least for it." Georgij kept his hands still. "I have a name. It is not written anywhere except in the book in my coat, and the coat is on that chair."

"How long?"

"A month. They have a new man and he has been through the room and through the people, and the ones who were worth anything were worth it because nobody had ever looked at them."

Annie turned round from the window then.

"So you have three days of records, one name out of two, a hole where the fourth ought to be, and a door that shuts in April."

"Yes."

"And it cost you Sang-hoon knowing that this house is interested in a book by the river."

"Yes."

"Now tell me about the desk at the door."

There it was, and he had known since the gravel that it was coming, and he had spent the drive deciding not to have an answer ready.

"There is a book at those things," he said. "Everybody who comes writes his name in it, and puts an envelope in the box, and the amount goes in the second column later in a different hand. I wrote my name. I had nothing for the box and I said so, and I asked the man to put a line through the second column."

Annie came away from the window and stood on the other side of the desk from him.

"How many men were near enough to hear you?"

"Thirteen. Four in front of me and seven behind, and two came up the stair while I was still at the desk."

"And how many of them will have it in a month."

"The man at the desk will have it for years. He has never had to draw that line before and it is a story he can tell at a table." He did not stop. "Of the other twelve, most of them by Friday. And two of them already knew who I was when I said my name, because they stopped talking."

"You have spent nine days making yourself into the one thing in this city that has no line and no owner and no date," said Annie. "This afternoon you wrote your name in a register with a date on it, at the door of a room with half that trade in it. Then you made certain that every man within hearing would remember which name it was."

"Yes."

"Do not agree with me. Tell me why you did it."

"Because the other version has a figure in it." He said it in the flattest voice he owns. "An envelope is money that is not mine, out of a house that is yours, and it goes into the second column under my name in a book that is kept. That is a number next to me, in ink, with a date. A line through it is nothing at all."

Annie put one hand down on the desk.

"That part is correct," she said. "It is the only part of today that is."

"In December you gave six hours to a woman who does not belong to you," said Georgij.

"I know what I did in December."

"You made a condition about how it was to be done, and the condition was that it must not be a gift, because a gift would have made her poorer and more careful." He did not hurry it. "What it did in the end was not take the threat off her. Nobody can do that. It took away the thing that made her worth threatening. The ground stopped being a designation and started being a rent, and the third charge on it stopped being a cliff in the spring and became a line in a schedule."

"The east side."

"The east side. That is the whole of the method and it is yours, not mine, and I have been doing nothing else since Thursday afternoon."

Annie waited.

"A page with four entries on it and one name known is a page with a queue on it," he said. "A page with four entries on it and all four dull is not worth carrying up a drive. I am not trying to take the book away from anybody. I am trying to make it not worth the postage."

"And you could not ask me first."

"No, Mistress. Not could not. Must not."

She did not move.

"Say the rest of it."

"The one thing in this that has any value at all is that nobody sent me." Georgij looked straight at her while he said it, because there was no version of it that survived being said to the carpet. "The moment you tell me to go at that register, it is your hand on it. You are the one person alive who cannot touch that book. Everything you do about it is an answer to a question nobody has asked yet."

"That is a good argument," said Annie. "Now say the flaw in it, because you have known it since the gravel and you have been walking towards it for twelve minutes."

The clock in the hall did the thing it does at the quarter, and neither of them looked at the door.

"I am the line," said Georgij.

"Louder."

"There is no such man as the one I have been describing. A page with four dull entries on it is worth nothing. A page with four entries on it, one of them attached to a man out of your house, is worth a very great deal. What makes it worth that is not the entry. It is that I have been walking round the city since March asking about it."

"And there is the second half of it, and it is mine and not yours," he said. "I have been doing all of this wearing a mark that is empty. Every man in that corridor read it and left me alone. Not one of them has looked."

"And this afternoon."

"This afternoon I made thirteen of them curious about the one book that would tell them there is nothing behind it."

Annie sat down at last, on the arm of the reading chair, which is not sitting.

"That is why I have not moved since February," she said. "It was not patience and it was not cleverness. There is no move available to me that does not confirm the line matters, and there is no man available to me who is not visibly out of this house."

"There is one thing that mends my half of it, and I am going to say it once so that it is not sitting in the room."

"Say it."

"You could have me put back in the book." He said it evenly. "A mark with something behind it works on everybody. A mark with nothing behind it works until one man checks."

"And."

"And it costs your name on a live page to do it. I looked at it on Saturday and I put it down. I am telling you so that you do not spend a week wondering whether I put it down."

Annie was quiet for a moment.

"My people in Yeouido could have had the dockets in two days," she said. "They would not have written their names anywhere. They are better at this than you are."

"They are much better at it than I am."

"Then give me the reason and make it a real one."

"Every one of them arrives from somewhere." Georgij turned his hand over. "They come in through a door and a diary and a fee, and a man like the one in settlement can see all three of those before he has finished standing up. Nobody comes over to them in a corridor."

"And somebody comes over to you."

"Twice he has tried to buy me, and both times he came to me to do it. Today he crossed a corridor to say it, in front of two men who wanted things from him."

"So the asset is that other men want you."

"Yes, Mistress."

She looked at him for slightly too long, the way Sang-hoon had, and unlike Sang-hoon she said it.

"That is a filthy thing to have to put in a report."

"It is the only true thing I have that is worth anything to you. I would rather it were the records work. It is not."

It was the only asset he had ever had, and it was not anything he had done.

Annie stood up off the arm of the chair.

"Bring me the coat."

He brought it and she did not take it. She waited until he had got the notebook out of the inside pocket himself, and waited again until he had opened it at the page. Then she read one line of his handwriting while he held it, and never put a finger on it.

"Keep it," she said. "It is no safer with me."

"Now the terms, and they are yours and I am giving them back to you." She stood where she was. "A ceiling. Named counterparties. A date after which it is dead and you come and ask me again."

"Mistress."

"The ceiling is that you do not spend yourself again without telling me the price first. Not the result first and the price afterwards, which is what I have had this evening. The price, before it is paid."

"And where there is no time to ask?"

"Then you decide, and you tell me the same night, and you tell me what it cost before you tell me what you got." She let that sit. "You have put those terms on other people since October, and you put them on me on Saturday. You know exactly how much they leave a man."

"Enough to work with."

"Enough to work with."

"The counterparties are Park Sang-hoon, the desk in settlement, and nobody else without my saying so. The date is the last day of March, because that is when your door shuts and I am not going to pay for a month you do not have."

Georgij put the notebook back in the inside pocket and the coat back over the arm of the chair.

"And the paper?"

Annie went to the drawer on the left of the desk, which he has watched her open perhaps four times, and put a folded document on the blotter and did not push it across.

"Mr Chae has had this since Monday afternoon," she said. "It is narrower than the one in December. It names three things and a month and it will embarrass you in any room that reads it properly."

"Then it is the right one."

"You asked me on Monday and I told you to ask again when there was a room in it." She put two fingers on the fold and left them there. "There is a room in it. There is a door, a name, and four weeks. I am not giving you this because you have earned it this afternoon. Some of this afternoon was very expensive."

"I know what it cost."

"You do not yet. You will in about a month."

Neither of them picked it up. It stayed on the blotter between them for the rest of the evening.

"The fourth one," said Annie. "The one with no car and no dinner."

"I have nothing on it at all."

"No."

And that was all she said about it.

She did not ask him what he thought it meant, and she did not ask him whether he had gone at it twice, and she did not ask him the second question. Annie asks second questions. He stood there with his hands at his sides and listened to her not ask it, and did the arithmetic, and put it where he puts them.

"Come here," she said.

He went round the desk. She did not have to say the rest of it, and he went down onto the carpet at her feet, which has stopped needing a word between them. Then she put her hand on the back of his neck the way she had on Saturday. This time she did not go past him and did not go on to anything else. After a while his shoulders came down about an inch, and he had not known they were up.

"You wrote your name in a book today," she said, above him.

"Yes."

"Put a line through it, you said."

"Yes."

"That was the correct thing to do and it was quick, and nobody taught you it." Her hand did not move. "I will not say that twice, and you are not to build anything on it."

He said nothing at all, which was not a decision.

Later, on the landing, he found that he had spent the whole twelve minutes of the report waiting for one particular sentence and that it had not come. Not once, in any form.

She had not asked him whether he would have told her if Jang had been in the kitchen.

She had decided not to find out. On the eleventh of March, about a man who has never said anything untrue in his life. Downstairs on the blotter there was a folded document with four weeks on it and no room in it for a second mistake.

# Book Two · Chapter 6: I have to ask
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.12 · EN

## Day One Hundred and Sixty-Four · Monday 16 March

He did not ask one person about the new man.

A man who is brought into a house to clean it out has cleaned out other houses, and those houses leave paper. Three of them, in six years. Two are still trading and one is not, and the one that is not filed everything it was ever going to file.

From that he got the order it comes in.

It is always the same order and it is not the order anybody expects.

The new man does not start with the desk that handles the money. He starts with the desk that handles the paper about the money, because that is where a house keeps the things it has decided not to write down properly.

And the tell, four to six weeks ahead of it, is a request in writing: would you set out, in your own words, how your filing works.

Nobody at a desk has ever read that sentence and understood it.

They sit down flattered and write four pages and hand over the whole architecture of their own protection, and six weeks later a man they have never met knows which drawer to open first.

Georgij knew the shape of it because he had built one in December.

He wrote that down on the Friday, in one line, and left it as it came.

He went over the whole thing on the Sunday with the three filings side by side and the dates in a column, in that order, before he decided he was going.

* * *

The house is a building near the river with a public stair on the west side.

He had been in it once, in October. He had come in at the back and gone down. He had been in the cellar of it for four hours with a number on him, and had not seen the front of the building until it was over.

He came in through the front door on the Monday at eleven and nobody stopped him.

He had settled that on the Sunday and did not open it again on the day.

In that building a clerk with a terminal can look up what is behind the thing round his neck. It takes under a minute, and what such a clerk finds is nothing. He went in anyway. There was no version of the month in which he did not.

Settlement is on the first floor at the end, past two rooms with nothing in them.

There is a counter with a glass panel above it and a gap at the bottom for envelopes. There is one chair on the near side, which tells you how long the average conversation is meant to be.

Mrs Jeon was behind the glass. She is somewhere near fifty. She has been at that desk since the house moved into this building, and her whole value for all of those years has been that nobody looked at her.

"I am not here to ask you for anything yet," said Georgij. "I want to tell you something first, and it is yours whether the rest of this goes anywhere or not. It will take four minutes."

Mrs Jeon had a receipt book open in front of her and did not close it.

"Four minutes."

He gave it to her in order and he did not hurry any of it.

Then the dates. Six weeks from the letter to the first desk, and about twelve days from the first desk to the second.

"And the second desk is this one," he said.

Mrs Jeon looked at him through the glass for a while.

"Why are you telling me this?"

"Because I am going to ask you for something in a minute, and I did not want to be holding it while I asked."

"That is the same thing."

"It is not, and you know it is not, or you would not have said it in that voice." He kept his hands where she could see them. "You have it now. You can send me down the stairs and you will still have it. That was the whole reason for the order I said it in."

She did not thank him.

That is not ingratitude. She had come in that morning with twenty-three years behind the glass and a job. She was going home that evening with twenty-three years and about two months. A man in a good coat had done that to her before eleven fifteen.

"Ask, then," she said.

"On the back page of the tidied catalogue there are four entries marked retained and not disclosed." He said it as though it were a shipping schedule. "I want to know who settled the oldest of them."

"You have seen the back page."

"I have a copy of the back page. It came up a drive in a flat parcel with a printed label on it, and so did one to every buyer on their list."

Mrs Jeon put one hand flat on the counter and left it there.

"You know what you are standing in," she said. "You know what this desk is."

"I know exactly what this desk is."

"Then you know what it costs a woman behind this glass to answer that question."

"I do not." He did not dress it up. "That is why I am asking you and not telling you. Say the price."

She took her time about it, which was correct.

"I want a name," she said.

"Whose?"

"Anybody's, so long as it is not out of this trade." She said it quite steadily. "In eight weeks I go out of that door with twenty-three years that I cannot put on a single piece of paper. There is no reference from this house that is worth anything anywhere. What I need is one person who will take a telephone call and say one sentence about me, and be somebody whose sentence carries."

Georgij did not answer.

He knew who he could ask before she had finished the second sentence. He knew what it was worth to her. And he knew that saying yes in that room would have closed the whole thing in under a minute.

He also knew what Annie had said in the small room on the Wednesday. *The price, before it is paid.*

"I have to ask," he said.

There is a particular silence that follows that sentence at a counter, and he had heard it before from the other side of one.

"You have to ask."

"I am not going to stand here and promise you a thing I do not own." He held her eye. "The name that would do this belongs to somebody else. I can go and ask for it today and I think I will get it. I am not going to say yes to you on the strength of what I think."

Mrs Jeon looked at him for what was probably four seconds.

"Sit down," she said.

He had been standing the whole time. He sat down on the one chair.

"Do you know how many men have stood on that side of this glass and promised me something." She had not moved her hand. "I do not mean this month. In twenty-three years."

"No."

"Neither do I, and I stopped counting when I was thirty." She let that stand. "Nobody has ever said the other thing. Not once, at this desk, in twenty-three years."

"I am going to give you one thing now," she said, "and it is not the answer to your question, and it is not a favour. It is so that you do not come back on Wednesday and waste both of our afternoons."

"The one thing."

"The oldest of those four never came through this desk."

Georgij sat very still.

"Nothing at all."

"No invoice, no receipt, no clearing, no line. I have been through it twice, because it bothered me at the time and it has bothered me since." Her voice did not change. "Everything in this house comes through this desk. That is the entire point of this desk. Somebody stood in that room and took a person home and this house did not send anybody a bill."

"And that is not a thing that happens by accident."

"That is not a thing that happens at all." Mrs Jeon took her hand off the counter at last. "Come back when you have your name, and I will tell you the rest of what I know, which is not very much and is worth having."

* * *

Mr Ku had the car on the far side of the street and did not ask.

He was home before three and did not start anything, which is not like him.

When the car came up the drive at twenty past five he went and stood in the small room, because sitting down in it would have been a way of putting it off.

"The price first," said Georgij.

"Go on."

"There is a woman at that desk who goes out of the building in eight weeks with twenty-three years she cannot write down anywhere. She wants one name. Somebody outside the trade who will take a call and say one sentence about her and be worth listening to."

Annie put the coat on the arm of the chair by the door.

"And you did not give her one."

"I have nothing to give her. I said I had to ask, and I came home."

"Say the obvious one first, so that we are not walking round it."

"Yours." He did not hesitate over it. "It would work in an afternoon. It would also put your name in that woman's mouth, in that building, eight weeks before she is turned out of it and has to explain herself to somebody. If anybody ever goes looking for a reason why this house is interested in that house, that is the reason, standing at a bus stop in Incheon with her handbag."

"Yes."

"So no."

"So no," said Annie.

She went to the window and did not draw the curtain.

"Park Sang-hoon."

Georgij had got there in the car and had spent the rest of the journey wishing he had not.

"He is on your list," he said.

"He is on my list because I put him there on Wednesday, and I put him there for this sort of thing and not for company." She turned round. "And he is the only name in this that explains itself. A man who buys and sells for a living has forty reasons to know a woman who does settlements. Nobody has to be told why he would speak for her. If it were my name, the only question anybody could ask is why."

"And what it costs," said Georgij, because she was not going to say it and it had to be in the room.

"Say it, then."

"It is the third thing he learns. He has the fact that this house cares about that book. He gets the fact that it cares enough to go to the counter. And he gets to be the man who fixed it, which with him is the expensive one, because he does not forget and he does not put things down."

"And it uses the corridor," said Annie.

He had given her that on the Wednesday in the middle of twelve minutes of other things, and she had kept the word.

"It uses the corridor," he said. "He offered it once and said he would not go on about it. This is not what a man means when he says that."

"It is exactly what a man means when he says that. That is why it costs."

"Do it," she said. "Today, not tomorrow, and not by telephone if there is any way of not using a telephone. And Georgij."

"Mistress."

"You will tell him what she is going to be able to say about him afterwards, before you ask him. He will say it does not matter. Tell him anyway."

He did it that evening. It took seven minutes. It cost precisely what he had said it would cost and produced precisely what Annie had said it would produce.

* * *

She was still in the small room when he came back, which she had no reason to be.

"It is the sixteenth of March," said Annie.

Georgij stopped just inside the door.

"Yes, Mistress."

"On the sixteenth of December I told you that I would ask you again, and that you would not be able to say it was not the moment." She did not get up. "It is the moment. Ask me for something."

He did not go round the desk.

He has gone down onto that carpet every evening for five days without a word being said about it. He stayed on his feet, because a man who asks for a thing from the floor is not asking for it.

"On the first of March I told you I was afraid of Tuesdays," he said.

"You did."

"I have had it every day since and it has not once got smaller."

Annie sat back.

"You gave me half of it on the first and I could not answer the half you gave me," she said. "Give me the rest."

"Before the nineteenth of February, being finished with me would have cost you weeks." He kept his hands at his sides. "A price. A room. People who would have had to be in it and a man like the one who was here at ten. Nine mornings of watching it happen, and somewhere around the ninth you might have found that you did not want to."

"And now there is nothing to sell."

"Now you can do it on a Tuesday, in a hall, between two other things, and it is finished before you get to the end of the sentence."

The small room did what a room does at half past nine.

"You paid seven weeks for that," said Georgij, "and four mornings in that building, and the third one was not about money. You did not know that was what you were buying." He did not soften any of it. "I knew on the morning you told me, and I said the cheap half of it and let you off, and I have let you off for fifteen days."

Annie did not help him.

"Then ask."

"Take Tuesday off me."

"That is a feeling and I do not buy those," said Annie. "Put it in a form I can act on."

Georgij stood in the middle of a small room and did the only thing left.

"Say that I am yours."

"There is nothing to write that on."

"No, and that is the whole of what I am asking for."

Annie did not move at all.

"In December I could not ask you," said Georgij. "You owned me. It would have been a slave asking not to be sold, and you would have had to answer it as one, and whatever you said afterwards would have been mine and not yours."

"And tonight."

"Tonight there is no paper on either side and I can walk out of this house on any morning I choose." He held her eye. "If you say it now, it is a thing you decided."

"There is a price in it and I am going to say it, because you would say it to me."

"Say it."

"You have never in your life agreed to a thing you could not close. There is a date on it, or a cap, or a named counterparty, and usually all three." Georgij did not stop anywhere. "I am asking for the one that has none of them, in a form that cannot be enforced and cannot be shown to anybody, so that you carry the whole of it and I carry none of it."

Annie was quiet for about eight seconds.

"There is a second half of that price and you have not said it," she said, and there was no accusation anywhere in it. "A man who is free and stays can afterwards stand in any room he likes and say that this house kept him. Since February there is no document on earth that would contradict him."

"That is correct."

"You are asking me to hand you that and then trust you with it."

"Yes."

"Say why I would."

"I have no answer to that which is not an argument," said Georgij, "and you would hear an argument. So I am not going to make one."

She got up.

She did not come round the desk, and she did not go to the window, and she did nothing at all with her hands.

"On the eleventh I told you that I would not say a thing twice and that you were not to build anything on it," said Annie.

"I remember it."

"You are mine."

Georgij did not say anything at all.

"It has no end on it and there is no Tuesday in it," said Annie, and her voice had not changed anywhere in the whole of it. "And I am not going to say it in a way that lets either of us call it something else in August. Build on this one."

"Yes, Mistress."

"Now come here."

He went round the desk.

He did not go to the side of it where he sits. He went down in front of her, where she was standing, which is a different place and which he has never done.

Annie looked at him from where she was for a moment and did not tell him to move.

Then she put her hand along the side of his face, cool from the room, the heel of it just under the bone.

He turned his head into it about an inch, which was the whole of what he did, and he did not say anything.

She has done that once before in her life. It was the twenty-ninth of December, in a hall, on her way past, and neither of them has ever mentioned it since.

After a while her thumb went once along his cheekbone and stopped, and neither of them said anything for some time, and the house did the things a house does at ten in the evening.

He went downstairs at about eleven and worked until twenty past one, because that was what the rest of the evening was for and neither of them was going to pretend otherwise.

What he did afterwards, on the Monday night, was the other half.

A settlement that never happened is still a fact about somebody. A house that does not send a bill has been told not to, and an instruction of that size comes from an owner.

The house has an owner. The owner is a fund, and the fund is four companies deep, and the fourth one is registered at an address in Jung-gu that also holds nine others.

He knew the shape of it before he was through the second layer.

He had seen it twice in the autumn, both times from underneath, both times without anybody's name at the end of it. It is not the ordinary kind of nesting. Somebody had built it to be dull, and had gone to a great deal of trouble to make each individual step look like the sort of thing a lazy accountant does.

So he stopped.

He did not order the fourth company's filings. He did not send for the register extract on the Jung-gu address. He did not put a single request into a system with a date on it, and he closed the whole thing at twenty past one in the morning and left it exactly as he had found it.

That was the correct thing to do and he did it quickly, out of the same instinct that had made him say *put a line through it* at a desk on the eleventh.

He had no way of knowing that it was the second time.
