He could have come in the car. Mr Ku offered twice and did not press it the second time, which is Mr Ku saying that he thinks it is a mistake.

A car of that kind at the door of a woman who has been out of work for seventeen days is a sentence about her, delivered to everybody on that stair. She would have had to live in it after he had gone.

Second floor. The bell has a strip of tape over the name.

She opened the door a hand's width with her hand still on it and looked at him.

"You," said Mrs Jeon.

"Yes."

She did not move.

"You do not have your name," she said. "I can see that from here."

"No."

"Then you have come to ask me for something on credit, and I told you in March what I do about that."

Georgij stood in a corridor with a strip light in it.

"May I have four minutes?" he said. "If you want me gone at the end of them I will go, and I will not come back, and nobody else will come here either."

She looked at him for what was probably three seconds. Then she took her hand off the door.

The flat is one room and a kitchen and a window with the eleven blocks in it. There is a table with two chairs, and on the table there is a school exercise book with a green cover and a biro lying across it, closed.

She had been sitting at it when he rang.

She did not put it away and she did not move it. She sat down in front of it with both hands flat on the cover, which is how a person sits who has decided that a thing is not going to be taken off the table.

"Four minutes," said Mrs Jeon.

"I have been in the house on the river since March," said Georgij. "I know what happened to your desk and I know who signed the schedule. I went and saw him yesterday afternoon and he told me about the ninth of January."

Her hands did not come off the book.

"He told you."

"He told me before he gave me your address, and he said out loud that he was telling me first so that it would not be payment." Georgij did not sit down, because he had not been asked to. "He said you had it in your hands and you were holding it out and he did not put his hand on it. He said every word of what he told you that day was true, and that it is still true, and that it is still the worst thing he has ever said to anybody."

Mrs Jeon looked at the window for a moment.

"He is not wrong that it was true," she said. "He could have opened it in January. He has had from January until May to be sorry about it, and being sorry about it is not the same as opening it, and I am not going to be the one who tells him it is."

"No."

"Sit down."

He sat down.

"Your four minutes have about ninety seconds in them," she said. "Say the thing you came to say."

"You were right," said Georgij.

Mrs Jeon did not answer that.

"Not you were probably right, and not there is something in it," he said. "The fourth reference on that back page is a person, and there was no bill because there was never going to be one. You went through it twice in twenty-three years because you were the only one in that building who could see the shape of it."

The biro rolled about an inch and stopped against her hand.

"You cannot know that," she said.

"I can."

"How?"

"Because a fee was paid for that line by the wrong man," said Georgij, "on the night, out of his own pocket, in an envelope that had already been made up. Nobody billed him and nobody was ever going to. He put a payment where an absence would have been."

She did not say anything at all.

"An empty space in a ledger is a question," he said. "A payment in a ledger is an ordinary Tuesday. He was not buying a deletion. He was buying the look of one, and he paid a house he did not owe in order to have it. The only reason anybody ever noticed the space was that a woman behind a glass panel could not let it alone."

Mrs Jeon put the biro down flat.

"I sat at that desk until midnight," she said.

Georgij waited.

"The one with no clearing. Four years ago, in the spring." She said it to the tabletop. "The room went at about half past ten and the runners were down by a quarter to, and at nine minutes past eleven they came and told me to keep the desk open, because there was a clearing coming. I kept it open. I sat there until midnight and nobody came, and in the morning I asked, and I was told that it had gone through the office instead."

"And it had not."

"It had not gone through anywhere." She looked up. "I have been in settlement for twenty-three years and that is the only night I have ever been told to wait for something that did not exist."

Georgij sat very still.

"Do you have the lot number?"

She did not open the book.

"You are asking me to give you the one thing I have," she said, "and I want to know what you are, because I have had three different answers about you since March and I have not believed any of them."

She put her hand flat on the cover again.

"A firm in Yeouido rang me on the twenty-eighth of April," she said. "A Miss Heo, who gave me her name and her extension and the house she was ringing for, and who was perfectly civil and had clearly been asked to be. I went in and sat in front of two of them and they were civil as well."

"And you did not take it."

"I had been told on the tenth that I was going. It was not announced, there is no register anywhere with my name in it, and there is nobody in that building who would put himself out for me." Her hand had not come off the cover. "So at the end I asked them how my name had come to be on their table. The pleasant one looked at the other one first, and then said that it had come through a contact."

Georgij put both hands on the edge of the table and left them there.

"Twenty-three years in settlement," said Mrs Jeon. "A line that arrives in the book and nobody will say where it came from is the one thing I know how to be afraid of. I have been sitting on one of those since January, and I was not going to go and work inside a second one for a salary." Her hand stayed where it was. "It was you."

"Yes."

"Then you may have the rest of the question," said Mrs Jeon. "You are somebody's. I could see that in March and I can see it now. Whose."

There it was.

He could have gone round it. There were three ways round it in the room and he could see all three, and the second one was good enough that she would not have found it for a week.

All three of them worked by making her somebody who is handled.

She has been that in a building for twenty-three years, and she was going to know.

"I am on that page," said Georgij.

Mrs Jeon did not move.

"The fourth of October," he said. "Two of the four references are that night. Lot eleven and lot fourteen, four lines apart. I was in the room for both of them, and I was one of them, and the one I was is the second one."

The flat was very quiet.

"You are telling me that to pay me," she said.

"Yes."

"Do you understand what you have just put on this table?"

She had asked him two questions since he came in and both of them had been flat. That one went up at the end.

"Yes," said Georgij.

"Then say it. I want to hear whether you have actually counted it or whether you are being generous at somebody else's expense."

"There is a woman who bought two people on the fourth of October," he said. "That page has four references on it and a phrase, and it has no column for who paid, and the house that wrote it is finished and cannot be asked anything. That is the whole of why she is safe."

"It went to every buyer in March," said Mrs Jeon.

"It went to six hundred and forty of them in March and it has been lying in their drawers ever since, because a page that nobody living will stand behind is a photocopy of an allegation." Georgij kept his hands where they were. "Mr Hwang can say the page is his. He cannot say who was in the room, and what he does know he knows because I told him in May."

Mrs Jeon looked at the closed cover under her hands.

"So I am the bill," she said.

"You are the bill," said Georgij. "You were behind the glass for both of them and there is nobody else left who was, and you are the only person in this who has never been paid by anybody. You could sell it. You could take it to a newspaper. You could hold it for eight years and take it out when you needed something, and there would be nothing anybody could do to you afterwards except things that would make it worse."

"And you did it anyway."

"I did it anyway."

He had handed her the one line that could end the house he lives in, because she deals in entries and he had nothing else that would clear.

Mrs Jeon sat back in the chair for the first time since he came in.

"Why?"

"Because you asked me for a name in March and I have not got one and I am never going to have one," said Georgij. "The only thing I have that a person in settlement would accept is a line on a page. You deal in entries. I have given you mine. It is not a favour and I have not made you a present of anything, and if you use it I will have nobody to blame."

She looked at him for a long moment.

"Twenty-three years," she said, "and nobody in that building ever told me anything that could hurt them."

She opened the exercise book.

It is not a ledger. It is a school exercise book with squared paper and a green cover, and there are about forty lines in it over twenty-three years, and every line has a date and a time and about six words.

She turned it round so that it faced him and put one finger under a line about two thirds of the way down the left page.

"Lot six," she said. "The spring auction, four years ago. Kept the desk open until midnight. No clearing."

Georgij read it twice and did not write it down.

"It was in the book," he said.

"It was in the book from the January before until the September after. I put four things through that desk against that reference in that time, and all four of them cleared, and they are on the line under it." She did not take her finger away. "Flowers, twice. A driver. And a doctor."

"A doctor."

"In the July." She got it out level and it cost her the same as it costs him. "I passed the invoice myself. It was a proper invoice from a proper practice, and I did not think about it for four years, and I have thought about it every day since the ninth of January."

Georgij looked at the line under it.

"Mrs Jeon."

"What?"

"I am going to find out what happened," he said, "and I am not going to promise you that it ends well, because I do not know and I am not going to say a thing to you that I would have to take back. What I will do is tell you. Whatever it is, and whenever I have it, you will hear it from me and not from anybody else."

She closed the book.

"That is the correct answer," she said, "and it is the first correct answer I have had from anybody since January, and I notice that it is also the only one that costs you something to keep."

She pushed the book about two inches across the table towards him and took her hand off it.

"Not to keep," she said. "Copy it and bring it back. I have had it for twenty-three years and I would like it in this flat."

She had given him everything in it and kept the book, which she had bought herself.

"I will bring it back on Tuesday."

At the door she said one more thing.

"There is a man in that building who is proud of keeping everything," said Mrs Jeon. "You may tell him from me that I kept mine too, and that I bought the book myself, and that it did not take a great deal of courage until the day it did."

Georgij went down two flights and out past the chemist and stood at the stop for a quarter of an hour.

The call was made. It was refused in the first minute it was possible to refuse it, and she was right to refuse it, and nobody would have had to explain any of that to him if he had asked once in April.

# Book Two · Chapter 28: A practice keeps records
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 4.0 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Thirty-Eight · Friday 29 May

He got back to the house at twenty past seven and went straight in.

There is an order in which a man can put an evening like that. The thing he came back with goes first, because it is very good, and the price goes at the end, when the room is already pleased with him.

He has used that order on other people this year and it works.

"I told her what I am," said Georgij. "Nobody gave me leave to do it. I did it at about half past ten this morning at a kitchen table four stops out, and I have not been able to make it not have happened since, and I have tried twice on a bus."

Annie was standing at the side of the desk with a folder open in her hand.

She closed it.

"Her name."

"Jeon Mi-ja. Fifty-one. Twenty-three years in the settlement office of that house, out on the twelfth of May, on the second floor of a block behind a chemist."

"What did you tell her?"

"That I was in the room for both of the October references, and that I was the second one."

Annie put the folder down on the desk and squared it with two fingers, which is not a thing she does.

"So there is a woman in this city who can put a buyer and a lot number in the same sentence and be believed," she said. "She was behind the glass when both of them went through, and there is nothing whatever standing between her and a telephone."

"Yes."

"And you decided that."

"I decided that."

The clock in the hall did the thing it does.

"Sit down," said Annie.

"I would rather not, yet."

"That was not a question."

He sat down.

She did not sit. She went as far as the window and stood with her back to the room for about ten seconds, and the drive was still light because it is nearly June.

"What did you get for it?"

"Lot six," said Georgij. "Four things cleared against it through her desk while it was in the book."

Annie did not turn round.

"Say the four."

"Flowers, twice. A driver. And a doctor, in the July."

She turned round at the doctor.

Neither of them said anything for a while.

"She passed the invoice herself," said Georgij. "She did not think about it for four years and she has thought about it every day since the ninth of January."

Annie came back and sat down at the desk after all, which she had not been going to do.

"A practice keeps records," she said.

"A practice keeps records."

"And a practice that saw somebody in July had to write something in the space where the name goes."

"Yes."

She looked at the closed folder for a moment.

"That is the first piece of paper in this entire business that was made by somebody who was not in the trade," she said. "Everything else has been made by people who know how to make it disappear. A receptionist in a practice does not know that and has never needed to."

"That is why I paid what I paid."

"I am aware of what you paid," said Annie. "I have been aware of it since the second sentence you said when you came in, and I have been doing arithmetic about it ever since, and I would like you to stop helping me with it."

He stopped.

She sat with both hands flat on the desk, which is his posture and not hers.

"You have had a sentence in your hand since Wednesday," she said, "and you have not put it on this table, and I have been waiting all evening to see whether you would."

"Say which one you think it is."

"That I held a name for sixty-eight days without leave, and that if you are going to be judged for deciding one thing about me, I can be judged for deciding one thing about you." She said it exactly. "It is a good sentence. It is worth about four minutes and it would have cost you the rest of the year."

"I know."

"Why did you not use it?"

Georgij sat in the chair.

"Because it is not the same," he said. "You held something back from me. I handed something of yours to a stranger. Those are two different verbs and only one of them can be taken away from the person it belongs to."

Annie looked at him for a long moment.

"That is the answer," she said, "and I want you to know that I checked."

She got up again.

"You were right about her," she said. "I have not met her and I do not know her. I am telling you that you were right, because you have been right about people for seven months and you were right about this one this morning. She is not going to use it."

"No."

"And it does not matter at all."

"No," said Georgij. "It does not."

"Say why, because I want to hear whether you have got there or whether I am going to have to walk you."

"Because she has nothing," he said. "A person with nothing has exactly one asset, and it is the thing she knows, and she does not have to be a bad woman for that to become the only door in the room. She only has to be fifty-one, and out, and in a market where nobody will read past the letterhead."

Annie stood in the middle of her own room.

"That," she said, "is the first thing anybody has got entirely right in this house since Wednesday."

She went round the desk and stopped.

"I am going to employ her," said Annie.

Georgij did not move.

"Not here, and not by me. The Gwangyang firm has a settlement function and it has been run out of a shoebox by a man's nephew for the last three years. I own half of it as of the eighteenth of May, and it is going to need somebody who has done twenty-three years of it properly."

"She will not take it."

"She will not take it the way it was offered to her in April, and she was right not to." Annie put one hand on the back of the chair. "She is going to be told who owns the half, by name, in writing, on the first page. And she is going to be told that the reason her name came up is that a man who works for me sat at her table this morning."

"That is in the commercial register and anybody in this country may go and read it," said Annie. "That is the whole of the difference between what I am about to give her and what you gave her at half past ten this morning."

"That is an enormous thing to hand her."

"It is the second enormous thing she will have been handed today, and she is going to notice that they came from the same house. She will work out inside a week that she has been made safe on purpose." Annie's hand stayed on the chair. "She may resent that. She is entitled to. She will still open the post on the first of the month."

Georgij sat very still and got there.

"You have just described what you did to me," he said.

Annie held his eye and took none of the weight off it.

"Yes," she said.

"On the fourth of October."

"On the fourth of October, at about ten past nine in the evening, for a sum I am not going to say out loud in a room you are sitting in." She said it without any weight at all. "You were the most dangerous thing in that building and you had nothing, and I have never once pretended to myself that those were two separate facts."

She had answered a question about a clerk in Gwangyang with the price she paid for him, and nobody had asked her for either.

The room was very quiet.

"Then I have not been punished," said Georgij.

"No. You have been corrected, which is worse, and you are going to feel it in about four days when you notice that I did the thing you should have done in April and that it took me eleven minutes."

He had no answer to that and did not look for one.

"There is one more thing and then you are finished for the day," said Annie.

"Yes, Mistress."

"You will not do it again."

"No."

"Say the whole of it. I do not want a piece of it turning up in September with a good reason attached."

"I will not give anything of yours to anybody without asking you first," said Georgij, "and if the room is such that I cannot ask, I will not give it, and I will lose whatever is lost."

"Yes."

She sat down at the desk and opened the folder again.

"Come here," she said.

He got up and went round and stood by the chair, and she put her hand up and took hold of the back of his neck, above the collar, and did not say anything for about six seconds.

Then she let go.

"Sit on the floor," said Annie. "I have four hours of this and you are going to be quiet while I do it."

He sat down at the side of the desk with his back against it, which is where he sat on Wednesday, and she picked up the pen.

He has been running since the eighteenth of March.

He has not stopped for one day and he has not been told to, and he has kept it out of the room by the ordinary method, which is not sitting down anywhere it can catch him.

The house was quiet and the pen went on and the light outside the window went orange and then went.

At about half past nine Annie put her hand down into his hair without looking, which she has done three times since March and which is becoming a thing that happens.

He said something with his eyes shut.

"What," said Annie.

"Nothing. It was not finished."

"Say it anyway."

"I was going to say that I do not mind being corrected by you," he said, "and then I heard the end of the sentence coming and I did not want to put it in the room while you are working."

Annie's pen stopped.

"Then do not," she said. "Not tonight, and not because I would not want it."

She went back to the folder.

Some time after ten she came to the end of a page and noticed that his breathing had changed. She looked down. He was asleep with his head against the side of the desk and one hand still open on his knee.

He has never done that in a room with her in it.

Annie sat with the pen in her hand and did not move her leg, because moving it would have woken him. She read on with one hand for another hour and twenty minutes and turned the pages with two fingers.

At about half past eleven she said one word out loud, to nobody at all.

"Yes."

---

# Book Two · Chapter 29: Nobody hides flowers
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 1.3 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Thirty-Nine · Saturday 30 May

He woke on the floor of the small room at about one o'clock with the lamp still on and a coat over him that is not his.

He copied the exercise book by hand between then and four.

There is a machine on the ground floor that would have done all forty lines in about a minute and put the time and the count in a log.

He has spent five months following one of those logs backwards through a building. He sat at the desk in the small room with a pen instead.

Forty lines over twenty-three years. A date, a time, and about six words.

He wrote them out in the order she keeps them and did not tidy any of it, and at about two in the morning he came to the line under lot six and stopped.

What she said out loud on Friday was four things. Flowers, twice. A driver. And a doctor.

What is written there is longer than that, because she is a settlement clerk and a settlement clerk writes down what she would need in order to find it again.

*6 Apr. 27 Apr. Hyoja-dong Flowers, house acct, both.*

*26 Apr, car, no letterhead kept.*

*3 Jul, practice, no letterhead kept.*

*All four cleared.*

She gave him more than she said out loud, and she said nothing about doing it, and she let him find it at two in the morning on his own.

Annie was at the desk at ten to seven with her coat back over the arm of the chair.

She is not up at ten to seven on a Saturday. Neither of them made anything of it.

"I would like the day," said Georgij.

Annie put the pen down, which she does not do for a question.

"For what."

"The flowers."

He put the copied page on the desk in front of her, the right way round, and stood back from it.

"There are three letterheads on that line and she wrote out one," he said. "Hyoja-dong Flowers, twice, on the house account."

"Why that one and not the other two?"

"Because that house bought flowers every week for thirty years and she could have written the name in her sleep," said Georgij. "The car was one invoice and the practice was one invoice. She saw each of them once, four years ago, and she wrote what she had."

Annie read the line twice.

"You said last night that the invoice from the practice was the first piece of paper in this made by somebody who is not in the trade," he said. "So is a delivery slip. A van had to go somewhere, and a man had to be told where, and somebody wrote the address down in the ordinary way."

"And nobody has thought about it since."

"Nobody has thought about it once. Nobody hides flowers."

Annie sat with the page in front of her for a while.

"Then here is what you are about to do, and I want you to hear it before you enjoy the rest of it," she said. "Every door you have gone through this year belonged to somebody who already knew what he was standing in. Byun knew. Hwang knew. Yeom knew before you sat down."

"Yes."

"That shop does not." She put one finger on the second date. "There has been a piece of paper in a cupboard in Hyoja-dong for four years and it has been worth nothing to anybody. At about half past ten this morning it is going to start being worth something, and you will be the reason, and it is the only copy."

Georgij stood on the other side of the desk.

"Then I will take the original in my hand and give it back to her," he said, "and pay for the copy, and say nothing at all about what is on it."

"Say the last part again."

"She does not get told what she has. The day she knows, she is a person who can be visited."

Annie opened the drawer and counted out notes and put them on top of the copied page.

"Take Ku and do not park in front of it," she said.

* * *

The shop is in a street of low buildings behind a hill in Hyoja-dong, third one along, with a green awning that has been mended.

Mr Ku put him down two streets away without being asked to, which is Mr Ku having listened to somebody in a hall at some point this week.

There are buckets in a rank on the pavement and a cold room at the back with a glass door, and the whole shop smells of cut stems and wet paper.

The woman behind the counter is about seventy and was doing the till roll.

"We open properly at ten," she said, and then looked up. "Come in anyway."

"Mrs Gwak?"

"That is on the awning. It has been on three awnings."

Georgij stood on the customer's side of the counter with his hands where she could see them.

"Four years ago this shop sent flowers twice on an account that has since been closed," he said. "The auction house on the river. I would like a copy of the two slips and I will pay for it."

Mrs Gwak put the till roll down.

"Is it true that they have shut?"

"Yes."

"Nobody rang," she said. "Thirty years of standing orders and one lot every spring and nobody rang to say. My son found out from a man who does the windows."

She stood there for a moment with her hand flat on the counter.

"What is your interest in it?"

"There is a person the flowers went to," said Georgij, "and I am trying to find out what became of them, and that is the whole of the truth about why I am standing here. I am not going to tell you the rest of it, because the rest of it is not mine to hand round a shop."

Mrs Gwak looked at him, and then at the cupboard behind him.

"You are the first person in a year to walk in here and not tell me a story," she said. "Min-a. The blue books, from the cupboard."

The blue books are duplicate order books, one to a year, with carbons, kept because an accountant said so a very long time ago and nobody has said otherwise since.

The girl went up a ladder and came down with four of them and put them on the counter in a stack that smelled of the cupboard.

Mrs Gwak found the year without looking at the spines.

"April," she said. "You said April."

She turned the carbons over from the back with her thumb, four or five at a time, and stopped.

"There."

The slip is a third of a page. There is a box for the order, a box for the delivery, and a box in the corner for who rang.

*6 Apr. Hyoja-dong Flowers. Twelve stems, white, no wrap.*

The delivery box has an address in Pyeongchang-dong, a flat number, and a floor.

Under it, in pencil, in a hand that is not hers: *Card: From an old friend.*

"That is my husband's writing," said Mrs Gwak. "He copied the cards into the book. He said a card is the only part of it anybody keeps."

Georgij read the corner box.

The name in it is Sim.

There is a telephone number beside it with the old city code in front, and the word *tel* underneath, because he had not come in.

"Turn to the twenty-seventh," said Georgij.

She turned four more carbons.

*27 Apr. Twelve stems, white, no wrap. Same as 6th.*

The corner box says Sim.

The delivery box has an address that is not in this city.

There is no card line on the second slip at all.

Georgij stood in a flower shop and read a box that was empty.

"He did not send a card the second time," he said.

"Then he did not send one." Mrs Gwak looked at where his finger was. "We ask. We always ask. If it says nothing there, he was asked and he said no."

Under the delivery box on the second slip there is a line in pencil in a third hand, small, the way a man writes when he is standing up.

*Left at the desk. They would not give a room.*

The shop was quiet and the cold room hummed.

"That will be Mr Han," said Mrs Gwak. "He drove for us for eighteen years and he wrote on everything. If a delivery did not go into a hand he put down why, because he was not going to be the man who lost a bouquet."

Georgij looked at the two slips side by side on the counter.

Three weeks apart. Two addresses. And between them, on her page, a car with no letterhead on the twenty-sixth.

Somebody was moved out of the city on the twenty-sixth, and the flowers went to the new address on the twenty-seventh.

The man who sent them did not have to be told where they had gone.

"Mrs Gwak."

"Yes."

"The man who rang. Sim." He had not touched either slip. "Do you remember anything about him at all?"

"I remember all of it," she said, "and I have never once been asked, and I have thought about it more than a florist ought to think about a telephone call."

She put her finger on the corner box.

"He was pleasant. He knew what he wanted and he did not want it explained to him." She said it the way people say things they have gone over. "And when he rang off the first time he said that it was good to see us again."

Georgij put one hand on the edge of the counter.

"We had never had an order from him," said Mrs Gwak. "Not once, and I looked, because I do not like being wrong about a customer. I sat here and went back three years."

"Say the sentence exactly."

"*It has been good to see you again.*" She got it out flat. "On the telephone, to a woman he had never spoken to in his life. And then twelve white stems and no wrap, twice, for somebody who was not allowed to have a room number."

The girl at the back put a bucket down and the water went over the tiles and neither of them turned round.

"Will you copy those two for me?" said Georgij.

Mrs Gwak took the book to the machine at the end of the counter and did it herself, and squared them and folded them once, and put the blue book back on the stack.

He paid for the copies and she gave him the change and he took it.

At the door he stopped, because there was one more thing and it was hers.

"You said your son found out from a man who does the windows," he said.

"Three weeks after."

"There is one man left in that building and he is doing the whole of it out of a spreadsheet," said Georgij. "Every supplier that house had found out the way you did. That is not a thing anybody decided about you."

Mrs Gwak stood behind her counter with the till roll in her hand.

"That is a kinder answer than the true one," she said.

"It is the true one. The kinder one would have been that somebody meant to ring."

He walked the two streets back to the car with the folded copies in his inside pocket and did not get in.

He has two addresses in his hand and he is not going to either of them today.

Pyeongchang-dong is forty minutes away and the second one is an hour and a half. He could be standing outside both of them before lunch, and he has been able to see the whole of that plan since the counter.

It is the plan he would have run in April.

He wrote in the notebook standing up, against the wall.

*Sim. Ordered by telephone, 6 Apr and 27 Apr. Says it is good to see people he has never met.*

*Yeom, four years ago, on the telephone: glad we had met. Two people who have never spoken to each other, one sentence.*

*6 Apr, Pyeongchang-dong, flat and floor. 27 Apr, out of the city. No card. No room number.*

*Car on the 26th. Doctor on 3 Jul.*

Then he stood with the pen still in his hand and wrote one more line, which is not evidence and is not for anybody.

*Somebody sent twelve white stems to a person nobody had ever billed, and then sent them again the day after that person was moved out of the city.*

Everything else that anybody wrote down in this was written by somebody who knew it might one day be read.

The only page in it with a person on it was written by a shop that had no idea it was writing anything at all.

Mr Ku had the car at the end of the street with the engine off and the window down.

"Home," said Georgij.

"You were fifty minutes."

"I was in a flower shop."

Mr Ku looked at his empty hands in the mirror and pulled out.

---

# Book Two · Chapter 30: Where the name goes
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 2.0 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Forty-Two · Tuesday 2 June

He came out on the bus again, which took fifty minutes, with the book in his inside pocket.

The tape is still over the name on the bell.

She opened the door the whole way this time and went back into the room without waiting for him, which is a different thing from Friday.

He put the exercise book on the table before he sat down.

"It is all copied and it is all there," said Georgij. "Nothing has been taken out of it and nothing has been added to it, and there is one copy and it is in a locked drawer in a house on the river."

Mrs Jeon put her hand flat on the green cover and left it there.

"You said Tuesday."

"Yes."

"Three people have said Tuesday to me this year."

She did not say what happened with the other two.

There is a letter on the table.

It has been opened along the fold with something thin, and the envelope is lying beside it, and both pages are lying face up where anybody coming into that room would see them.

She has put it where he would have to look at it.

"Sit down," said Mrs Jeon.

He sat down.

"It came on Saturday," she said. "First delivery. Somebody paid for that, because nothing comes to this street on a Saturday."

"Yes."

"Two pages, and four of terms behind them. A settlement function in a firm in Gwangyang that has been run out of a shoebox by somebody's nephew. Twenty-three years wanted, terms above what I was on, and a start date I may choose myself."

She turned the first page round with one finger so that it faced him, the way she had turned the exercise book round on Friday.

"There is a name on the first page," she said. "It is a woman's."

"Yes."

"Say it."

Georgij said it.

He has heard that name said out loud in a great many rooms this year, in boardrooms and on a gravel drive and by men who were frightened of it.

It has never once sounded the way it sounded in that kitchen.

Mrs Jeon sat back.

"And underneath it there is a paragraph that tells me why my name came up," she said. "In writing. It says a man who works for her sat at this table on the twenty-ninth of May, and that I may ring the number at the bottom and ask them anything I like."

"Yes."

"When did you know?"

"On Friday evening," said Georgij. "She said it in front of me at about half past eight and it was decided by a quarter to nine."

"And you were out here on Friday morning and you did not come back on Saturday."

"No."

Mrs Jeon looked at him across her own table.

"Why not?"

"Because it is not mine," he said. "She decided it, and it is her firm and her name on the page and her money. If I had come out here on Saturday to tell you first, I would have taken a thing that belongs to her and used it to be liked by you." The flat was quiet. "And you would have read that letter on Saturday morning as a thing I did, and you would have been right to."

She did not thank him for that.

"I have been handled," said Mrs Jeon.

Georgij did not go round it.

"Yes."

"Do you know how many times in twenty-three years I have been handled by that building." She put both hands on the table. "I know the shape of it in the dark, and I have been reading this since Saturday morning, and it is the shape."

"It is."

"Then say the difference, because there is one and I want to hear whether it is the same difference I have got or a worse one."

Georgij sat with his hands on his knees.

"You can check every word of it," he said. "Who owns the half is in the register and anybody in this country may go and read it. The reason your name came up is on the page in front of you and it is the true reason. And the number at the bottom belongs to people who will answer it whether they have been told to or not."

"And that is not the same as being asked."

"No. It is not the same as being asked."

She let that sit for a moment.

"In April I was rung by two civil people who would not tell me how they got my name," she said. "In May I was made redundant by a man who has never once looked me in the face. On Saturday I was handed the best thing that has happened to me in four years by a woman I have never met, and every single one of those three was decided in a room I was not in."

She put the second page back on top of the first.

"I am fifty-one," said Mrs Jeon. "I have four months of money and a son who is going to offer next month, and I am going to take it. And I would like it understood by somebody that taking it is not the same as being asked either."

"It is understood."

"By her?"

"She said it before the letter was written," said Georgij. "She said you would work out inside a week that you had been made safe on purpose. She said you would be entitled to resent it and that you would open the post on the first of the month anyway."

Mrs Jeon looked at the wall for a while.

"That is a horrible thing to be right about," she said.

"She has been right about me for eight months."

She had not asked him anything about himself, and he answered as though she had.

"And how do you find that."

"Some of it I have not got round to yet."

She poured water into two glasses without asking whether he wanted one and put one in front of him, which is the first thing she has given him that was not owed.

"You have come for something else," said Mrs Jeon. "You would have brought that book back by courier if it was only the book."

"There is one thing I did not ask you on Friday."

"Ask it."

"The invoice from the practice." Georgij put his glass down without drinking from it. "I asked you what it was. I did not ask you what it looked like."

Mrs Jeon put her glass down.

"I have been waiting since Friday for somebody to ask me that," she said, "and I did not know it until you said it."

She did not go and get the book. She has not needed the book for any of this.

"It was not a bill for a consultation," she said. "It was an attendance. A doctor went to a place and saw somebody there, and there was a line for the travelling on it and the travelling was more than the attendance."

"How much more?"

"About three times." Mrs Jeon turned her hand over on the table. "I remember it because it is the only medical invoice I have ever passed where the getting there cost more than the seeing."

Georgij sat very still.

"It was not in this city," he said.

"It was not in this city."

"And where the name goes."

Mrs Jeon looked at the table between them.

"There was a box for it," she said. "Every invoice from a practice has one, because they are paid by insurers and the insurers want a person. This one was not going to an insurer. It was going to a house that settles lots."

"What was in the box."

"A reference," said Mrs Jeon. "Six characters. The same six that were on my clearing slip, which is the lot."

The room did not do anything at all.

"Somebody in a practice was given a lot number and told that it was the patient," she said, "and wrote it in the box where the name goes, and sent the bill to the auction house, and was paid inside the month. And I passed it. I looked at that box and I read six characters and I put it through and I went to lunch."

She had both hands flat on the table again.

"That is the ninth of January," she said. "That is what I went upstairs about. Not the four years. The lunch."

Georgij left the notebook in his pocket.

"You are not asking me where," said Mrs Jeon.

"No."

"Why not?"

"Because you are going to be inside a firm that belongs to her by the middle of the month," said Georgij, "and the less of this that is in you, the better that is for you. You have given me a lot number and four cleared items and I have got what I needed out of that on Saturday. I do not need the rest of it from you and I am not going to take it because it is available."

Mrs Jeon sat with both hands round the glass.

"On Friday you gave me a thing that could take her apart," she said, "and today you will not let me give you an address."

"Yes."

"Those two do not go together."

"They go together perfectly," said Georgij. "On Friday I had nothing else to pay you with. Today I have. That is the only thing that changed and I am not going to dress it up as a principle."

She looked at him for a long moment and then, for the first time in either of the two mornings he has spent in that flat, something at the corner of her mouth moved.

"You are a very strange young man."

"I have been told."

He got up to go at about half past eleven and stopped with his hand on the back of the chair, because there was one more thing and he had been carrying it since Thursday.

"Mrs Jeon."

"What?"

"Mr Hwang asked me for something and I did not answer him," said Georgij. "I want to give you the question instead of deciding it, because he asked me to arrange a thing about you without asking you, and I have had five days to notice what that is."

She waited.

"He said that if it turned out you were right in January, he would like there to be a piece of paper somewhere in the world. One that says you sat in that room and held the book out, and that he did not take it." He said it as nearly as he could remember it. "Not for him. He said he is finished and he has understood it properly. He said he would like it to exist."

Mrs Jeon did not answer for a while.

"He wants it to exist," she said.

"Yes."

"Then it will exist and I will write it," she said, "and he does not get to have it."

She granted it exactly as he had asked for it, and took it out of his hands in the same sentence.

She got up and took the two glasses to the sink.

"I will write one page and I will sign it and I will put the date on it," she said with her back to him. "And it goes to you, because you are the one who came out here, and because a thing like that is worth nothing in the hand of the man it is about."

"I will keep it."

"You will keep it and you will not use it, and if you ever do use it you will find that I am extremely difficult."

"Yes."

At the door she said one more thing, and it was not about any of that.

"Tell her that I read all four pages of the terms and that the third one is generous in a way that somebody thought about," said Mrs Jeon. "And tell her that I noticed it was posted on Friday night."

He went down two flights and past the chemist and stood at the stop.

Friday night.

She wrote it, signed it and had it out of the house before eleven o'clock on the night he came home and told her what he had given away.

Eleven minutes, she had said, and about four days.

It is the fourth day and he is standing at a bus stop with the whole of it in front of him at once. She heard the worst thing he has done to her this year, and she took eleven minutes, and inside those eleven minutes she solved the thing he had put a line through in March and not looked at since.

He has not been punished. He has been shown.

The bus came and he got on it and sat at the back with the empty inside pocket.

He thought about a woman going to lunch, four years ago, after she had put a bill through for a person with six characters where the name goes.

---

# Book Two · Chapter 31: The drawer that locks
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 6.0 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Forty-Three · Wednesday 3 June

He put everything on the desk before breakfast, in the order it had come to him and not the order that made him look best.

Byun's folded sheet. Hwang's compliments slip with the address on the back. The copied page from the exercise book. The two flower slips. The notebook, open at the right page.

Annie stood over it for a while and did not touch any of it.

"You have not shown me this before," she said.

"No."

"Why now?"

"Because on Friday I promised you something and I have been keeping it by accident since Saturday," said Georgij. "Since the flower shop, the only money that has gone into this is what you already handed me yourself, and I have not used your name once. I only noticed this morning that both of those were decisions, and I had not told you I was making them."

Annie sat down and picked up the flower slips first.

She read them twice.

"Sim," she said.

"Yes."

"Say what you know about him and not what you have guessed."

"That he is not Choi Dae-ho. He is the one Choi Dae-ho tells to make the calls," said Georgij. "The man who wanted it hidden had a fee paid for him rather than let anybody know he could have had it for nothing. That is a man who has somebody else telephone a flower shop, and is careful never to be in the room when it happens."

Annie put the slips down.

"And the two addresses."

"Three weeks apart. The first one is a flat with a number and a floor. The second one will not give a name at a desk." He kept his hands flat on the edge of the desk. "Somebody was moved, and moved to somewhere with a desk that says no."

"A desk that says no is one of three things," said Annie. "A ward. A facility that takes people nobody wants found. Or a house that has been told to say no by somebody who pays its bills and does not live there."

"I had got as far as the first two."

"The third is the one that matters, because it means the desk is not protecting the person inside it. It is protecting whoever is paying for the silence, and the person inside it may not know that is what is happening to them at all."

The house was quiet.

"You have not gone to either of them."

"No."

"Say why, and I want the true one, not the one that sounds like restraint."

Georgij stood with his back straight.

"Because I do not know who is paying for the desk that says no," he said, "and every other man in this has been somebody I could stand in a room with and outlast. Byun is finished. Hwang is finished. Yeom sold and got out. Mrs Jeon has nothing left to lose that she has not already lost. I have been walking into empty buildings and cold flats all year and calling it work."

"And this one is not empty."

"This one has been paying to keep a secret for at least four years and has never once had to explain himself to anybody. I do not know what that kind of man does when a stranger stands in his corridor and says a true sentence at him."

Annie looked at the notebook, open on the desk, and did not read it upside down, because she does not need to.

"So you brought it to me instead of finding out."

"I brought it to you because if it goes wrong, it does not go wrong to me alone," said Georgij. "It goes wrong to whoever I work for, in whatever room I am standing in when it happens. I have spent eight months learning that the hard way about other people's names. I did not check whether it was also true of mine."

Something in her face did not move and something behind it did.

"That is the first time you have said that sentence in this house," said Annie.

He had said that he has a name, and he had said it as a hazard and not as a possession.

"I know."

She stood up and went to the window, the way she had on Friday, and stood with her back to the room.

"I am not going to tell you to stop," she said. "I watched what you did with a similar decision on Friday night and I want you to keep doing it. But I would like it understood, once, properly, and not while you are standing at a bus stop working it out for yourself afterwards."

"The rule, then."

"You do not go near either address without telling me first," said Annie. "Not asking. Telling. I am not going to be the one who says no to this, because it is not mine to say no to. But I am not going to be the one who finds out from Ku that you did not come home either."

Georgij stood very still.

"Yes."

"And you are going to let me put somebody on the second address before you go anywhere near it," she said, turning round. "Not to protect the desk. To find out who is behind it, from outside, in a way that does not put your name in front of anybody until we know what we are looking at."

"That is slower."

"It is a great deal slower, and you are going to do it anyway. You have just spent five minutes telling me that the reason you have not gone is that you do not know what you are walking into, and the answer to not knowing is not to walk in faster."

He had no argument for that and did not look for one.

"Yes, Mistress."

Annie's mouth moved, very slightly, at the second word, and she did not comment on it and neither did he.

She gathered the papers into one stack, squared them, and put them in the drawer that locks.

"Copies," she said. "You keep the notebook."

"Yes."

Annie held one page back before the drawer went shut.

"And the page from Mrs Jeon. The one for Hwang."

"I have not looked at it since she gave it to me," said Georgij. "It is not addressed to me and I am not going to read it as though it were."

"You are keeping something you have not read, and that is either very disciplined or very frightened," said Annie. "I am not certain which, and I do not think you are certain either."

He did not answer that, because she was right and he had not decided.

"There is also Sang-hoon's four," she said. "He gave you a task in a shed last week and I have heard nothing about it since, and I notice that you have brought me everything except that."

"Because I have got nothing on it," said Georgij. "Four decisions a man cannot account for, and I have been looking in every direction and finding a woman in a kitchen with a school exercise book instead. It is not the same investigation and I have let it eat the time that belonged to the other one."

"Then say that to him before he says it to you."

"I intend to."

He got as far as the door, on his way to whatever the morning had been going to be before he emptied his pockets on her desk, and turned round.

"Thank you," he said. "For not asking me why it took until this morning."

Annie closed the drawer and turned the key.

"I already know why," she said. "You wanted one clean week where nobody in this house had to forgive you for anything. You very nearly had it."

"I know."

"Go and have your coffee before it is cold," said Annie, "and send Jang up to me on your way past the kitchen. Do not tell him what for."

He did not ask what for either. That is a thing he has learned to do only since Friday, and it cost him something to do it standing in that room. It would have cost him nothing at all on a bus.

Jang was in the kitchen doorway with a cup he had not started on, which is a thing Jang does when he has already decided to go somewhere and is waiting to be told to.

"She wants you upstairs," said Georgij.

"Now."

"Now."

Jang put the cup down without drinking from it.

"You are not coming."

"No," said Georgij. "This part is not mine yet."

"Coffee's on the stove," said Jang, in the way a man does when he has decided not to ask a question, and went.

Georgij stood in the kitchen on his own and poured a cup he had been told to have, and it was, in fact, nearly cold.

* * *

---

# Book Two · Chapter 32: Two witnesses
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 6.0 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Forty-Four · Thursday 4 June

He could not sleep and did not try very hard.

At about one he took the notebook downstairs and read it from January forward, which he has never done in one sitting, because a page read on its own day never looks like the page next to it.

*Yeom, four years ago, on the telephone: glad we had met. Two people who have never spoken to each other, one sentence.*

He had written that on Saturday and underlined nothing, because on Saturday it was one fact among many.

Eleven pages earlier, in different ink, from a shed with a hull in it:

*He tells people he is glad they have finally met. The first time. When they have never met.*

*Have you ever watched him eat.*

Georgij sat at the small table with both entries open in front of him.

He read them across from each other for a long time before he let himself think the sentence, because the sentence, once thought, does not go back into the notebook.

*Now it does not need her to have been right alone.*

He has known since the twenty-seventh of May whose habit this is. Annie has known since she was thirty, and before that since she was fourteen, and neither of those is a thing that can be shown to anybody. A daughter's memory is not evidence. It is the truest thing in the house and it would not survive a single hard question from a stranger.

What sat on the table in front of him at one in the morning was not a name. It was two people who had never met Choi Dae-ho in their lives, four years and one telephone call apart, describing the same six words in the same shape. Two witnesses who owe him nothing and have never heard of each other.

He made himself take it apart before he trusted it, the way he would have taken apart anybody else's claim.

Two people, four years and one telephone number apart, who each told a stranger they had never met that it was good to see them again. That is a habit, and habits are not evidence. A habit shared by two different men is a coincidence. A habit that specific, said in that exact shape, twice, four years apart, to a florist and to a businessman who had never laid eyes on the caller either time, is not a coincidence twice.

He wrote nothing new in the notebook. He sat with the two old pages open and let the rest of it arrive on its own, because it does that faster when it is not chased.

Byun: paid from a pocket, in an envelope already made up, so that the money would be in the right place and nobody would ever have to explain where it had come from.

Yeom: given a position that paid more than the house was worth, in a winter when somebody had been asking for two years, and never once told who he was working for.

Sang-hoon: eight years of dinners with a man who has never eaten in front of him and four decisions he has never been able to account for.

A man who arranges other people into rooms and does not sit at the table himself.

A man who pays to have his own name kept out of a ledger four years after the fact, because being owed nothing was worth more to him than the money he spent proving it.

A man whose only mistake in this whole business is a sentence he cannot stop himself from saying to strangers. It is the sentence he uses on everybody, and he has said it so many times that it has worn a groove.

That groove is the first piece of Choi Dae-ho that has ever left a mark somewhere other than in Annie's own memory of a room she was not old enough to be allowed into.

There is a third thing, and it took him longer to find because it was not in either page. It was in what both men had been holding when the sentence landed.

Mr Yeom, on a telephone in his own house, had never met the caller and never would. Mrs Gwak, behind a counter she has stood behind for thirty years, had never had an order from him before that morning and went and checked. In both rooms the sentence was aimed at somebody who had absolutely nothing to compare it against, and in both rooms it worked anyway, because a compliment that cannot be checked is the only kind that is never wrong.

Georgij sat in the small room until the window went from black to grey.

He went up at half past six and Annie was already awake, which she should not have been either.

"You did not come to bed," she said.

"No."

He put the notebook on the desk, open at the two pages, and did not say anything else until she had read both of them.

Annie read them the way she reads everything that matters, twice, and the second time slower.

"Say it," she said. "I want to hear you say it before I say it, because if I say it first you will spend the rest of the morning deciding whether you agree with me instead of telling me what you actually think."

"It is him," said Georgij. "I have known that since the twenty-seventh of May, the same as you." He put one hand flat on the desk. "What I have this morning that I did not have then is two people who have never heard of each other saying the same six words in the same shape. Neither of them was told to say it by us."

"That is not nothing."

Annie kept her eyes on the page.

"It is not proof of anything I could take to a room full of strangers, but it is a great deal more than I have ever had. I have carried this since I was fourteen years old and I have never once been able to hand it to another person and have them check it for themselves. This morning I can."

Annie sat with both hands flat on the desk.

"Say what it actually gets us," she said, "because I do not want to sit here being moved by it before I know what it does."

"It gets us two witnesses outside this house who can independently describe the same man, without either of them knowing the other exists." Georgij kept his hands where she could see them. "It gets us two addresses and a doctor who was paid through a lot number, and none of that was written down by you or by me. It does not get us a court. It gets us the first thing in twenty-four years that is not only your word."

"Yes."

"Then the florist is not safe either," she said.

Georgij had not got that far and it went into him properly.

"No," he said. "She is not."

Annie stood up.

"Nobody goes near either address today," she said. "Not you, not Jang, not anybody. Every person who has touched any part of it in the last week is a name he could reach for if he ever works out what has been asked and by whom. I am not going to find out how long his reach is by testing it with people who work for me."

"Mrs Jeon."

"Starts at a firm with my name attached to the deed in eleven days, and I am going to move that up if I have to." She was already at the door. "Mrs Gwak."

"Sells flowers in a street she has sold them in for thirty years and has no idea what she gave me."

"Keep it that way."

She stopped with her hand on the frame.

"You are not to tell Sang-hoon that any of this has gone further than it had in the shed," said Annie. "Not the florist and not the addresses. He already has the man. He does not get the rest of it yet."

Georgij looked at her for a moment before he answered. The last time he had held a piece of information back from a man who had asked him for it, it had cost him a great deal to say so out loud, four days ago, in this same room.

"He asked me for the four decisions. This may touch one of them."

"It may touch all four of them," she said, "and that is exactly why. If you hand him a florist and an address he cannot yet protect, in a week where he has already told you he will not be useful to you again this year, he will act on it. He will act before either of us has decided what acting on it should look like." She looked at him. "That is not something either of you can take back. You said it yourself on Wednesday. If this goes wrong, it does not go wrong to you alone."

Georgij stood very still.

He has been the one deciding when to move since March. Byun's door, Hwang's crates, Mrs Jeon's kitchen table, the counter in Hyoja-dong. Every one of those rooms he walked into on his own clock. Every one of them he could afford to be wrong in, because the man on the other side of the table had nothing left to do to him.

This was the first time in eleven weeks that being told to wait was not an insult and he still had to make himself hear it as anything else.

"You are telling me to sit on the best thing I have found in five months."

"I am telling you to sit on it for four days," said Annie, "while I find out three things you cannot. Who else has been at that man's table. What he actually owns behind the lawyers in Singapore. Whether anybody has ever once seen him lose." She let that sit. "Then you may do whatever the four days have made possible."

"And if it comes to nothing."

"Then you will have cost nobody four days that mattered," she said. "And if it comes to something, you will have cost him four days he did not know he was being given, which is the only kind of head start anybody has ever had on a man like that."

She went out.

Mrs Seo came in with coffee he had not asked for and put it down without comment. It is a thing she has done exactly twice this year, and both times it was because somebody in the house had not been to bed.

"You are not going to tell me," she said.

"No."

"Good," said Mrs Seo. "It is easier to run a house for people who do not tell me things than for people who tell me half of them." She looked at him for a moment on her way to the door. "Drink it before it goes cold. You did that yesterday as well."

She went out and left him with the cup and the notebook.

Georgij sat down at the desk with the notebook still open at the two old pages.

He read the entry from the shed again, in his own handwriting, from a week ago.

On the day he wrote it he had already had the name for two days. He had still needed Sang-hoon to say it, in a room with a hull in it, before it felt like a fact and not a thing Annie had believed since she was a child.

He drank the coffee, which had already started to go cold.

He thought about a woman in a flower shop who had gone back three years in her own order book because she did not like being wrong about a customer. She had answered every question he put to her without once asking what it was for.

She had trusted him because he had not told her a story. He had not thought, until this morning, to ask himself what he had actually asked her to carry.

The girl who had gone up the ladder for the blue books. The husband who used to copy cards into a register that nobody but a stranger would ever read again. A driver who had spent eighteen years writing down where every delivery went, and had no way of knowing that one slip of it would be worth what it was worth to anybody.

None of them had asked for any part of this. All of them had, without knowing it, corroborated a fourteen-year-old's memory that nobody had ever been able to check.

He wrote one line and closed the notebook.

*Four days. Not hers to lose either.*

He did not mean Annie when he wrote it.

* * *

He had written the line at about eleven and sat with it for a quarter of an hour before he let himself notice which woman he had meant instead. Then he put the notebook in the drawer and went up.

There was a light under her door.

There has been a light under her door on perhaps forty nights this year and he has knocked on about nine of them. On the other thirty-one he has stood in a corridor for a moment and gone to his own room, and neither of them has ever mentioned it.

He knocked.

* * *

She was on the small sofa with a book she was not reading and her shoes off, which is the only untidy thing she does.

"You have been down there since seven," she said.

"I have."

"Do not tell me about it."

Georgij stopped just inside the door.

"Again."

"Do not tell me about it. Not tonight." Annie closed the book without marking it. "You have brought me something every evening for eleven days and I have taken all of it. Tonight you came up the stairs with your hands empty and knocked anyway, and that is what tonight is going to be."

He stood in the middle of her floor and found that he had nothing arranged for it.

"Then I do not know what to do," he said.

"No," she said. "I know. Sit down."

He looked at the chair.

"Not there."

He sat down on the floor with his back against the sofa, on her side of the room, and it took him longer than it should have, and she let it.

He has sat on the floor at the side of her desk since the eleventh of March. He went down onto the carpet at her feet that evening without being told to, and neither of them has said anything about it since. It is where he sits. Nobody in this house has ever remarked on it, including him.

"You did the arithmetic on the stairs," said Annie.

"I did."

"Say it, and then we will have said it and it will be over."

He put one hand flat on the carpet.

"In my fourth week I worked out where in a room it is cheapest to be, and I have done it in every room in this house every day since, and I do it now without noticing." He did not look up. "I noticed tonight. I got as far as the third step."

"And then what."

"And then I came up anyway and knocked anyway, and I am telling you that I did it, because you would know if I did not."

Annie did not say anything to that.

She put one hand into his hair, at the back, and left it there.

She has done that four times since March and every one of them happened while she was looking at something else. This time there was nothing in front of her.

He did not move at all.

There is a thing he does in every room he has ever been in. He keeps one way out inside his field and he prices the distance to it. He has done it since he was nineteen and does not know how to stop. He stopped. He could not afterward have said at what point in the hour it went.

They stayed like that for a while, and the house did the things a house does at half past eleven.

Somewhere below them a door was shut carefully by somebody who did not want to be heard shutting it. A car went past on the road, and then, after a long time, another one.

She did not ask him anything.

That is the part he could not have described to anybody afterward, and did not write down, and has thought about since. A woman who asks four questions a minute for eleven hours a day sat in her own room for the better part of an hour and asked him nothing at all.

"May I ask you for something?"

Annie's hand stopped.

"You have asked me for three things in eight months," she said. "A piece of paper. A room with nobody else in it. And a woman in Ulsan." Her hand had not moved. "Ask."

Georgij sat with that for a moment. She had put them in the order they happened and had not needed any time at all to do it. And she had counted the one he called the smaller one on the bridge, which he had assumed she would have let go of by Christmas.

He looked at the wall opposite rather than at her.

"On a bridge in November you gave me something and told me it was on nothing and that I could not spend it." He kept his hand flat on the carpet. "I have not said it since. Not out loud, not in this house, not once. And I have not been sure for six months whether it was given to me or shown to me."

"And you have gone six months without asking."

"I have gone six months without needing to know," said Georgij. "That ran out on the third step of your stairs."

Nothing happened for about three seconds.

He heard her put the book on the arm of the sofa.

Then she came down onto the floor beside him, without any of the noise a person makes doing that, and sat with her back against the same sofa and her shoulder against his arm.

She did it before she answered him. He understood the order of those two things about a second afterward, and in seventeen years it is the only occasion on which an answer has arrived before the words for it.

"Say it," said Annie.

He said it.

He had not had it in his mouth since a bridge in November. He had been afraid of getting it wrong, in the way a man is afraid of a thing he has not admitted to being afraid of. He did not get it wrong.

Neither of them said anything for a while.

"On the first of March I sat at a window against your legs," said Georgij, eventually, "and it was the best evening I have had since I was nine years old. You were in a chair."

"I know. I was in it."

"I have sat on a floor in this house nearly every day since March and you had never once been on it." He did not move his hand off the carpet. "I have thought about that chair a great deal more than I have thought about the window, and I was not going to tell you that, and I did not ask you for this."

"No," said Annie. "You did not, and you would not have, and both of us knew that four minutes ago." Her shoulder stayed where it was. "You have spent eight months in this house on the understanding that nothing arrives in it that you have not first worked out how to be worth. I am not going to argue with you about that tonight. I am going to sit here instead, which is quicker."

After a while she reached over and put two fingers under the collar, at the side, where the skin is.

She has never done that.

She has put her hand on the back of his neck twice in February, on her way past and on her way to something else. Again on the eleventh of March, and that was the first time she did not go on to anything. In the study on the twenty-seventh of April, flat against the side of his neck, and then she sent him to bed. On Friday for about six seconds, and she said nothing at all while she did it.

Every one of those was above it.

She has never touched the thing itself, in either direction, in eight months, and he had assumed until this moment that it was a decision she had made in the first week and had not revisited.

It is warm, because it has been on him since the second house.

"Does that hurt," she said.

"No."

"Say the true answer rather than the fast one."

Georgij closed his eyes.

"It has not hurt since the third house," he said. "It is warm. That is all it is. It is the only part of me that is always the same temperature and I have not thought about that in about nine years."

Her fingers stayed exactly where they were.

"On the first of March you told me that this is not what holds you," said Annie.

"I did."

"And then you told me what it does hold." Her fingers did not move at all. "I said it stays on and you said it stays on, and neither of us has been back to it in three months, and I have not stopped thinking about it since. Not about taking it off."

"About what, then."

"About the fact that you had it worked out in the second week of October and carried it round until March without spending it."

Georgij did not open his eyes.

"There was no afternoon in that autumn in which saying it would have been anything other than a demand."

"There was one," said Annie. "You picked the one morning on which I could not answer it with paper. I said so at the time and you did not deny it."

"It was on purpose," said Georgij. "It was the only morning in five months on which saying it cost me something instead of buying me something. That was the whole of the reason and I have not been sorry about it once."

Her fingers came out from under the collar and went back to where they have been before, at the back of his neck, above it.

"Yes, Mistress," he said, because that is what he says.

"Not to that one."

She put her hand into his hair and left it there, and neither of them said anything for a long time.

* * *

He went to his own room at about one, because she did not tell him not to and because he did not ask, and both of those were choices and both of them knew it.

At the door he stopped, and she was already looking at him.

"You did not tell me what you found tonight," she said.

"No."

"Good. It will still be there in the morning and so will I."

He wrote nothing at all in the notebook that night.

The first page has an entry for every single day since the eleventh of March, and there is a gap on the fourth of June, and he has never explained it and is not going to.


---

# Book Two · Chapter 33: Whose four days
*Lot Fourteen* · Version 6.0 · EN

## Day Two Hundred and Forty-Five · Friday 5 June

Sang-hoon telephoned at ten past nine, which he has never done before in eight months, because Sang-hoon does not telephone.

"You are not at your desk," said Georgij.

"I am in a car. Say that I woke you."

"You did not."

"I have had nine days of thinking about a sentence I said to you in a shed," said Sang-hoon, "and I would like to know whether it has produced anything." He did not pause for an answer. "I am asking on the telephone because I am not going to be in a room with you again until Tuesday, and I do not enjoy waiting."

Georgij stood in the corridor with the receiver against his ear and did the arithmetic he had already done twice that morning.

He can say that he has movement. He cannot say what it is.

Sang-hoon already has the name. Saying it again on an open line, next to flowers and a street in Hyoja-dong, would put a shape around a woman who has no idea what she gave him. He cannot let that sentence, said whole, arrive on a telephone a day before Annie is ready for it to.

"There is movement," said Georgij.

"Say the shape of it."

"I cannot yet. Not because I am protecting you from it and not because I am protecting myself. There is a third party in it who has not been told anything is happening, and if word of this reaches the wrong table before she is somewhere safe, it goes badly for her specifically."

The line was quiet for a moment.

"A woman."

"Yes."

"Is she one of the four?"

"No," said Georgij. "She is somebody who could get hurt because of how close she has stood to this without knowing it, and I am not going to spend her safety to satisfy your Tuesday."

Sang-hoon made a sound that was almost a laugh and was not one.

"That is the first time in eight months you have told me no on the telephone," he said. "You have always found a way to make it sound like yes with conditions."

"This is yes with conditions. The condition is four days, and it started yesterday, and I am not going to move it because you rang."

"Whose four days?"

Georgij stood with the receiver against his ear and did not answer straight away, because the true version of the answer would tell Sang-hoon exactly what he was not supposed to be told.

"Not entirely mine," said Georgij. "I am not going to say more than that on a telephone, and I would rather you thought worse of me for saying too little than better of me for anything else."

Sang-hoon did not answer straight away, and the car noise on the line changed, which meant he had turned a corner or a page.

"That is a very expensive way to talk to a man who has just given you a name for nothing," he said. "Four days, then. Tuesday. Not before."

"Not before."

"And if it is what I think it is."

Georgij stood with his back against the wall.

"If it is what you think it is," he said, "you are going to have to decide something about eight years of your own life, and I am not going to be the one who chooses when you do that either. That is the other reason for the four days, and it is not the smaller one."

There was a long silence that was not the car.

"You are a strange thing to have working for somebody else's house," said Sang-hoon, "and I mean that as the compliment it very nearly is." The line clicked once. "Tuesday."

He rang off without saying anything further, which is not a thing he does, and Georgij stood in the corridor with the receiver still warm in his hand.

Mrs Seo passed with a tray and did not stop.

* * *

Georgij went and found Annie in the room off the library, where she keeps the papers that are not in the desk that locks, and told her all of it, in order.

She listened without writing anything down.

"He asked whose four days they were."

"Yes."

"And you told him the truth before you had decided what it was."

"Yes. I said not entirely mine, because that was the only true thing available in the time I had, and I have not worked out since whether it was also the whole truth."

Annie looked at him for a moment the way she had looked at the notebook on Wednesday, which is to say properly.

"And what did it cost you to answer that honestly, instead of saying mine and letting it stand, which is shorter and which nobody could have disproved."

"A question I do not have an answer to yet, about whose four days they actually are," said Georgij, "and I would like to know that myself before Tuesday."

Annie set the papers down.

"They are mine," she said, "in the sense that I am the one who can afford to spend them and you cannot. They are yours in the sense that you are the one who will have to live in whatever room comes after Tuesday. I do not think that divides as cleanly as either of us would like it to."

"No," said Georgij. "I do not think it does either."

She went back to the papers, and he stood there a moment longer than the conversation required.

For the length of one telephone call that morning he had been, without deciding to be, exactly as careful with the truth as the book he keeps in his own head says a man is allowed to be. It had not felt like a technicality even once.

He wrote nothing about it in the notebook. Some things, he has learned this year, are worth more left where they happened.

* * *

Jang found him in the garage corridor an hour later, in the coat he wears when he means to be outdoors and has been told not to go.

"I have not been to the second address," he said. "I want that said out loud once, by me, so that if it matters later it is on record who said it and when."

"It is on record. I heard you say it."

Jang stood with his hands in his coat pockets and did not take them out.

"I had a route worked out by Wednesday afternoon," he said. "A tradesman's approach, a reason to be on that street that would not survive a second look but would survive a first one, which is all it needed to. I have not used it and I am not going to, and I would like to know how long that is going to sit unused, because a plan that waits too long stops being current."

"Four days from Wednesday. Tuesday."

"That is not an answer to my question."

Georgij looked at him properly.

"No," he said, "it is not, and I do not have a better one, because I do not know myself what Tuesday actually produces. I know what it is supposed to produce. I do not know that it will."

Jang took that the way a man takes an answer he has had to give himself more than once in his own career.

"Eight families," he said. "I have waited on worse instructions than this one for worse reasons, and I have never once been told why by the person giving them, and I have got used to that being how it works. I am not asking you to change that."

"Then what are you asking."

"I am asking whether the person you got it from is the sort who wastes four days, or the sort who spends them." Jang finally took his hands out of his pockets. "Because I have worked for both, and they look identical from where I am standing, and it has cost me a great deal over the years to find out which one I had after the fact instead of before."

Georgij thought about that for a moment before he answered, because it deserved one and not a reflex.

"She spends them," he said. "I have watched her do it since October and I have never once seen the four days come back empty. I am not saying that to be loyal. I am saying it because it is the truest thing I have got to give you in place of a reason."

Jang nodded once, the way he does when a figure has been confirmed rather than offered.

"Good," he said. "I did not need the reason. I needed to know whether the wait was being run by somebody who knows what waiting is for."

He went back up the corridor toward the house.
